While the crooked occasion has not yet come together, one breeds a mind of fantasy and delusion; when there is no device to entice, one breeds a mind of scheming; at the least hindrance, one breeds a mind of anger and hate; when desire is topsy-turvy, one breeds a mind of greed and attachment; envying what another has, one breeds a mind of jealous poison; to seize what another loves, one breeds a mind of killing. Shame and honour are utterly lost, and the bonds of human relation all fail. Every kind of evil karma is born from this, and every kind of good thought dies from this. Now when the lustful mind stirs but once, though no deed has yet been done, one has already piled up evil and made guilt to this degree. How much more for him who openly treads and plainly practises it?
The law of the underworld says: He who violates another man's wife shall have the retribution of a line cut off. He who violates a maiden shall have the retribution of lewd and dissolute children.

The proverb says: I urge you, sir, not to borrow the debt of romance; what is borrowed quickly must be quickly repaid. In your own house there is one who will pay it for you; when you would repudiate it, he will not repudiate it.

He who kills a man kills but his one body; he who violates a woman kills her three generations. For he not only breaks that woman's chastity: he makes her husband's parents, her husband, her sons and daughters hang their shame on their brows and feel the pain to the very marrow. It may even come to death from shame: the husband kills his wife, the father hangs his daughter, the son will not acknowledge his mother, kin find no face to show, and decent families will not join with them in marriage. For a moment's stolen pleasure, he creates guilt that fills the heavens, and the retribution of a line cut off is still not enough to cover his offence.

Only when there are husband and wife are there father and son, elder and younger brother. He who violates a woman throws into disorder not only the one relation of man and wife, but the relations of father and son and of brothers as well, and so three of the five relations perish. It may even bring on his ancestors the pain of offerings that are not accepted from an alien line. How can the execution of gods and the slaughter of ghosts be escaped?

He who kills a man destroys that which is his after birth; but he who violates a woman throws into disorder that which is hers from before birth. Besides, he who kills a man hates him. But as for him who violates a woman, what hatred has he against her husband, her husband's parents, or against that moth-browed beauty herself, that he must needs defile her body and destroy her chastity?

When lustful thoughts are many, good thoughts must be few; when lustful thoughts are few, good thoughts are of themselves many. Therefore he in whom lustful thoughts are wholly dissolved obtains three of the five blessings: length of years, health and peace, and a good end. He in whom lustful thoughts constantly arise must suffer the affliction of sickness and the calamity of an untimely and cut-short death.

A moment's desire is easily dissolved, while the rank and life of a whole career weigh very heavy. Why then in bitter toil should one throw away a hundred years of name and honour, a whole lifetime of prospects, the accumulated merit of one's forefathers, and the blessing and emolument of one's sons and grandsons, for the bewilderment of half an hour? I truly do not know what manner of lungs and bowels such a man has. There are further those who flee in terror and fall ill, and cannot be cured by any medicine; who are bound fast and ruin their households, and lick their own navel too late. Worse still, when the intrigue is exposed, they stake their head for a moment's pleasure; and by the round of retribution they pay off the debt of romance with their own wives and daughters. The misery of it is past telling. Take warning at once.

The saying goes: Lewdness draws near to killing. It is true. Yet to say it draws near to killing is still a mild word. I hold that where there is lewdness there is never a case without killing. If the husband learns of it, he seizes a knife in his fury and kills. If a fellow in the intrigue is jealous, he sets his keen blade to the man and kills. If death comes of the lewdness, then the king's law kills him. If he is lucky enough to slip through the net, then the aggrieved ghost kills him. If he escapes all these, then consumption and deep-seated disease, past even Bian Que's healing, and the Lord of Destinies kills him. A man, with the most spiritual and most precious body of action between heaven and earth, sets himself in a place where he must surely be killed. How foolish, how pitiable.

Ri Gan Chu She says: In ancient times there was a worthy who, when lustful thoughts blazed up, put his hand into the fire; the pain was past bearing, and the lustful thoughts died. If they did not die, he would calm his mind and sit in silence, seeing his body as already dead. And again, he would send his spirit to the graves of the ancients, and think thus: This man in the world was as I am; I in the grave shall be as he is. What is the joy of lust?

The guarding of the mind against lust rests wholly on the power of wisdom. Duke Di Liang of the Tang once said: When dazzling beauty is before a man, let him think quickly that this woman will one day sicken and die, that her corpse will rot and gather worms, and that the stench will assault men's noses. Dreadful and fearful as it is, the crooked thought is straightway loosed.
The Song of the Skin-Bag by the Patriarch Bodhidharma of Liang says: A ditch of urine and dung, a heap of pus and blood — reckon it up: what joy of romance is there in it?

The Patriarch Lü of the Tang said: Do not boast that in youth you follow romance; you only run the rounds of rebirth and peddle bones. If you do not believe it, look into a bright mirror: beneath the skin of the face is a skull. He also said: The fair maiden of sixteen has a body soft as cream; at her waist she wears a sword that slays the foolish man. Though you do not see the head fall, in secret it dries his marrow to the pith.

The Method of Guarding against Lust says: She entices me to kill myself and ruin my house, to shorten my years and break my blessing; she is in truth a thing that takes my life. One should look on her as a sharp blade that kills a man, as a tiger or a wolf, as a venomous snake, as a ghost-messenger that hooks away the soul, as an enemy from a former life. If one holds such contemplations, it is like bringing water to quench fire: the lustful thought cannot but die.
Gao Zongxian of the Ming said: This body is like white jade; one false step and it is shattered. This matter is like bird-poison; one taste of it and one dies.

Men today are often misled by the one word love, not knowing that the word love was given us by Heaven for loyalty and filial piety, for friendship and brotherly affection, for kindness to the people and love of creatures. Used rightly, it makes a sage; used wrongly, it makes a beast. May one not fear it?

A Daoist book says: The offence of violating a woman exceeds that of killing a man by several degrees. It also says: However a man may practice austerities and cultivate, all his offences may be dissolved — save only that he who has broken the virgin body of a maiden cannot be released hereafter, though his Way be high and his practice full. He must first receive an evil retribution before he can attain to truth.

The Buddha said: If a man in the world does not violate the wives of others, and his mind does not dwell on crooked and perverse things, he obtains five good rewards. First, he does not lose his wealth. Second, he does not fear the magistrate. Third, he does not fear men. Fourth, he is born in heaven, and the jade maidens of heaven become his wives. Fifth, coming down from heaven he is born again into the world with a wife of great comeliness. That some men today are comely and fair of feature is owing to this: in former lives and by past destiny they did not violate the wives of others. If a man in the world is lewd and dissolute, and violates the wives of others, he obtains five evil rewards. First, his household is not at peace and he often loses wealth. Second, he fears the magistrate, and has constant dealings with the rod and the whip. Third, he deceives himself, and his body is always in fear of men. Fourth, he enters the hell of Mount Tai, where the iron pillar is red-hot and he must ever embrace it, because he violated the wives of others, and so obtains this calamity; and for tens of thousands of years his punishment is not ended. Fifth, when he comes out of the prison he is born as a fowl, a duck, a bird, or a goose, lewd and dissolute, without avoiding even mother and son, and with no restraint at all. The horse keeps ritual and the wild goose keeps chastity, and both have the foot of faithfulness; but the fowl and the duck are lewd and dissolute, and alone have no limit or measure. All this is because in former lives and by past destiny they were lewd and dissolute and violated the wives of others, and so received the body of a fowl or a duck, and are ever eaten by men. Such toil and bitterness cannot be numbered or told.

The Buddha set out the five precepts. The first is not to commit sexual misconduct, which brings the reward, in this life and the next, of parents and kindred who are long-lived, healthy, and harmonious, and of wives and daughters who are chaste and good.

The Sutra of Retribution says: A certain ghost asked: I have received this body, and by nature I am full of terror; I am ever in fear that men will come to seize and shut me up and bind me, and to add to me every cruel torture; I have never a joyful heart. What offence has brought this? The answer was: When you were a man, you were fond of sexual misconduct and violated the wives of others. You were forever thinking that it would be found out, and your heart had no peace. Now you receive the flower-retribution, and the fruit lies in hell, where you shall lie on a bed of iron or embrace a pillar of copper. Such guilt cannot be reckoned or told.

Emperor Wen's Record of Heavenly Warnings says: He who violates the wives and daughters of others and defiles their inner chambers shall suffer in hell five hundred kalpas before he can be released to birth, and shall be born as a mule or a horse; and after another five hundred kalpas he shall again receive a human body, as a prostitute or a player. He who violates and lies with widows or nuns and ruins their conduct shall suffer in hell eight hundred kalpas before he can be released to birth, and shall be born as a sheep or a pig to be slaughtered by men; and after another eight hundred kalpas he shall again receive a human body, blind or mute, or maimed and crippled in the five features and the four limbs. He who throws the bonds of human relation into disorder by the base violating the noble and the young the elder shall suffer in hell one thousand five hundred kalpas before he can be released to birth, and shall be born as a snake or a rat; and after another one thousand five hundred kalpas he shall again receive a human body, and shall die in his mother's womb or perish in the arms of a nurse, and shall never enjoy a long life. The retribution for the offence of lust is pitiable indeed.

The Admonitions of the Women's Quarters says: The guilt of lewdness in a woman can never be washed away all her life; no filial son or loving grandson can ever cleanse it. Therefore the good woman and the lady of name keep their persons like jade, and cannot bear the least flaw. Should they meet with a wild fellow, they must on the spot throw the shuttle and refuse him with sternness, and he will naturally not dare offend again. Such is the upright spirit of the fragrant chamber, which gods and ghosts protect. And if a woman is lewd and disorderly, will she have no evil retribution? The law of the underworld punishes it with rebirth as a dog or a swine; and it is not merely that in the world of the living she is spat upon and reviled. Let this too be a warning.

The easiest place for any man to lose his footing is when dazzling beauty is before him and he cannot master himself in that blazing moment. At such a time there are three demons. The eye falls on her face, her bewitching looks crowd into the heart, the bones burn and the spirit flies, the smoke rises and the flame blazes: this is called the fire demon. The root of desire stirs, the Ren and Du channels secretly open, like a dyke about to burst, like a sluice about to break: this is called the water demon. Fire and water boil each other, form and spirit tumble together, like a wheel that never rests, like a ring that has no end: this is called the wind demon. These three demons are three passes. To cut through the three demons and cross the three passes there is no other way: there is one sword of wisdom, and it is called forbearance — firm forbearance, and fierce forbearance. To go hungry rather than eat the tiger's leavings, to go thirsty rather than drink poisoned wine: this is the teaching of forbearance. To wrest the knife from two men fighting and not let go though blood flows, to seize the road though the army is broken and not turn back though the arrow strikes: this is the teaching of firm forbearance. When the viper bites the hand, the strong man cuts off his wrist; when the poisoned arrow strikes the flesh, the hero scrapes the bone: this is the teaching of fierce forbearance. At such a pass, if one can hold firm and endure through, then one moves heaven and earth and stirs gods and ghosts, and one's merit is rounded and one's practice fulfilled. But if a single thought lingers and turns back, one's grasp must become unsteady. Those flowers by the wall and willows by the road, the powdered white and painted green, in the turning of an eye become emptiness; and by this one's allotted years are taken away, by this one's emolument is reduced, and by this one may even lose one's life. And if his destiny be wealth and honour, he shall be poor and lowly; if his fate be peace, he shall meet calamity and change; if by his portion he should have sons, his line shall be cut off; and he who hoped for noble sons and worthy grandsons shall beget the base instead. Moreover there is the retribution of hell, the retribution of future lives, the retribution of the brute creation, the retribution of wives and daughters who are lewd and dissolute, the retribution of descendants in poverty, the retribution of prostitution and play-acting. A single thought straying a little brings boundless poison and pain. Alas! Dare one not forbear? Alas, alas! Dare one not forbear?

The first thing in checking lust lies in the daily work of instruction and gradual influence by fathers and elder brothers, teachers and friends. One must make a man deeply believe that to wrong one's conscience in a dark room is known, and that the eye of the god is as lightning; and that in his breast the law of ritual, the law of cause and effect, and the retribution of calamity and blessing are not doubtful by a hair. Then of himself, when the occasion touches him, he will wake with a start and turn the light of his mind about, and will not be careless at the moment of trial.

In the haunts of wind and moon most men lose their footing and sink half their lives away, and looking at their own shadow are ashamed and afraid. To find one who keeps upright and is unstained — how many can there be? All day long they vow not to be lewd, yet the lewd mind burns the more; to every man they speak of curbing desire, yet the seed of desire grows the more. They give rein to passion and never turn back, and bring on themselves the full measure of ruin. Truly, if one is deluded at first and awakes at last, then calamity departs and blessing follows. Master Xie Shangcai of the Song said: The way of Heaven brings calamity on the lewd, but not upon the man who repents his offence. That saying is true.

Since the retribution of lust is so heavy, the merit of guarding against lust and the guilt of leading others into lust must have retributions that are not light. I pray that every man may put forth the blue lotus of his tongue and wield the coloured brush on his desk to make known these responses and retributions, to save and pull out those deluded by lust, to circulate them far and wide, and to teach and guide one another in turn. Whether in a great assembly with solemn words, or in a private room with bitter counsel, do not fear mockery, do not shun the charge of being a musty pedant; persuade them gently and earnestly, and you will surely make your hearers wake to deep reflection and receive benefit without end. Thereby to turn back the mad tide of moth-browed beauty that cuts down a man's nature, and to give the good medicine that brings the embroidered ranks to turn their heads — is this not to love men with virtue, and to seek abundant blessing for oneself?

Among the mouth-karma of men today, there is none worse than to delight in talking of the women's quarters, relating lewd and foul matters, with every kind of guessing and elaboration, one singing and a hundred joining in. Often because the speaker savours it, the hearers are set all aflutter. Now the secret wickedness of lewdness truly concerns a man's name and honour for life: one word carelessly let fall brings endless calamity and entanglement, and provokes the wrath of Heaven more than anything else. How much better to speak constantly of the retribution of chastity and lewdness, and to uphold the teachings of name and the bonds of human relation, and so obtain blessing from Heaven?

The Record of Heavenly Warnings says: He who composes lewd books and corrupts men's minds shall enter the uninterrupted hell after death, and shall not be released to birth until those books are utterly destroyed and the guilt and retribution of all who did evil because of them are made void.

Yuan Liaofan of the Ming said: He who takes lewd and filthy books, foul pictures, and slanderous words and burns them shall have the reward of sons and grandsons who are loyal, filial, chaste, and righteous. He who delights to read lewd tales and novels, who recounts the stories of lewd books, and who keeps lewd books and lewd pictures in his house shall have the reward of sons and grandsons who are prostitutes and players.

The chapters of Turning Back the Mad Tide from the Sea of Desire record many teachings on guarding against lust, set out in clear order and class by class, with warnings suited to each occasion. Because that book is too narrow to carry them all, a selection is appended here.

A maiden is at the age when she waits in the women's quarters to be betrothed; it is the beginning of her name and honour for a whole life. If one destroys this conscience of hers and ruins her name and honour, then her parents and all her kindred hang their heads in shame and lose their colour. And even if someone should take her in marriage, it is very often found out, and she is sent back as before; and it often comes to rage and shame, and the loss of life itself. Even if the marriage is brought off in secret, she wears a hidden fear ever after. Her great chastity is already impaired, and for a thousand autumns it can never be washed clean. Every man who has a human heart should first of all sternly abstain.

A widow who keeps her resolve is revered by gods and ghosts and honoured by the court with public praise. If one ruins her bitter chastity, then while she lives she has no face in the world of the living, and when she is dead she grieves the more bitterly in the springs beneath. Let a man try to turn and picture it: will he not be chilled at heart? It is right indeed to spare no pains to preserve her, and to let her achieve her name and keep her chastity whole. Then the virtue one plants is all the thicker; it is not merely that one has refrained from lust.

Is a maidservant not also a maiden? I would have my own daughter chaste: can I then ruin the chastity of another man's daughter? And a servant's wife is another man's wife too. I would have my own wife keep her chastity: can I then make another man's wife lose hers? Noble and base have their ranks, but name and honour are the same. How can one destroy one's heart and deeply offend against the retribution of the unseen world? Moreover, the jealous wife whips and beats her and wounds her life; the violent servant answers back and betrays his master; father and son, unknowing, become beasts in one herd; brothers in mutual delusion share one bed; or a child of one's own flesh and blood is degraded to a low concubine, and later generations in their ignorance do shameful things to her, while in name she stands as maid or mistress, but in the hidden world there is the grief of brother and sister. To wound the manners and corrupt the customs is more than I can bear to speak of. How is it that men find lewdness easy to practise, and are so calm and unguarded?

The wet nurse ranks among the eight mothers, and the nun quietly keeps the Buddha's ground. To offend against them is to make sin within sin. The present punishment of the law and the private calamity are, to be sure, the lighter part.

That a woman disappointed in love should run away lewdly, or teach lewdness to win favour, does sometimes happen. Never think that because she comes to you it is unfeeling to refuse her. If one passes the test at such a time, one's virtue is thick and one's character rare, and Heaven will surely witness it, though one does not seek to be known of men. This is the pass between good and evil and the border between calamity and blessing; here above all one should strive.

To take one's pleasure with courtesans seems to be no offence; yet one falls into their snare, and often ruins one's house. Moreover one's parents cast one off, kin and friends grow distant, wife and children hate one; one is cut off from the bonds of human relation and loses the keeping of one's jade. It may go so far that sores infect the body, that the eyebrows fall and the nose is eaten away, so that there is a body with no whole skin left. There was a friend of mine whose privy parts rotted away, who said of himself that for one mad hour he had suffered the punishment of castration for life, with his line cut off and his body maimed, and wept and repented too late. And there was another man of Huizhou who was infected with a foul pox, and the son he begot was red flesh without skin, and did not live. Alas. Men say it does no harm to one's hidden virtue; who knows that it is no different from suffering the condemnation of the underworld? Strictly abstain, strictly abstain.

The Six Things Not to Be Done concerning male lust says: In lewd defilement and indecent dalliance, the face wears a shameless look; reverence is lost, and the sense of shame is extinguished. This is the first. You cast off the wife of your youth and dote on a youth; perverse breath brings strange offspring, and love and hate are turned awry. This is the second. Such fellows are frivolous and reckless: what conduct can they keep? They steal jade and filch fragrance, and the men of the house are infected. This is the third. Three feet above your head there is surely a god; he is angered at the filth and sends down no light punishment. This is the fourth. The statutes record the sin of sodomy, and the king's law is plain; and lewdness again draws near to killing, and life itself is at stake. This is the fifth. It seeks no offspring from you, but recklessly wastes your essence; foolish is this traffic, and it swiftly takes a man's life. This is the sixth.

I exhort all men everywhere: those who have not yet offended must hold to the precept with trembling care, shun ill and seek good, and keep all their lives the precept of not knowing a second colour. And those who have already offended must think urgently of mending their ways and greatly doing good, printing books that warn against lust and exhorting men far and wide, to atone for their former fault. So may they turn calamity into blessing.

In former times Yao Tingruo of Tongcheng printed and gave away a form of vow and precept, saying: Of the hundred virtues, filial piety is first; of the ten thousand evils, lust is the chief. Man differs from the birds and beasts in what he keeps in his heart. The wild goose is a flying bird, yet it does not throw its flock into disorder. Man bears the four virtues: how is he not the equal of a bird? Therefore we take refuge and vow to abstain from sexual misconduct. Should this thought sprout, calamity falls upon the body; should this precept be broken, woe reaches the sons and grandsons. We pray only for your compassion to pity us and witness our vow, to protect and uphold us and secretly aid us, and to keep us safe from life to life. All who receive this form shall gather a few like-minded men, write out these eighteen lines on a separate sheet, together with their native place, each writing his own name and signing it, and burn the vow before the Lord of the Dipper, or before Emperor Wen, or before Lord Guan, or before all the Buddhas, and keep the precept for ever without forgetting it, and vouch for one another every year. After a few like-minded men have made the vow and the precept, let them at once contribute to print ten thousand copies of this form and give them away, so that good method may be handed down without cease. At the end of the form, several maxims and retributions must be appended.

I have gathered the various teachings as above, so that exhortation and warning are complete, and both the model and the prohibition are set out, now in gentle words, now in urgent cries, in clear phrases and earnest meaning. If a man can read it from hour to hour and ponder it from moment to moment, he will surely be one who gains. Yet, taken up as they came to hand, I am still ashamed that their order is not well arranged; let the reader but grasp the purport. I shall still set out in full below the retributions of chastity and lewdness, to aid urgent awakening.

A certain student of Guixi failed the examinations again and again. He begged Master Zhang, the Celestial Teacher, to send up a memorial and search the heavenly roll. The god wrote in reply: This man's portion should be a degree, but it has been taken from him for stealing upon his aunt. The reply was reported to the student, who said it was not so. He then sent up a document to plead for himself. The god wrote again: Though the deed was not done, the thought was truly there. The student was ashamed and repented beyond remedy. It was because in his youth he had seen his aunt's beauty, and for a moment a single thought had stirred.

Zhao Yongzhen of the Zhengde era of the Ming, when young, met a man of strange gifts, who said: At twenty-three you will certainly be sent up as the first graduate. When the time came for the provincial examination, his essay was exceedingly good, and the examiner had fixed him as first for several days. Then, unexpectedly, there was an error in the later sessions, and he did not pass. His heart was full of discontent, and so he prayed for a dream before Emperor Wen. The emperor said: In this examination you should indeed have been first. But lately you have dallied with a maidservant and enticed a neighbour's daughter. Though no lewdness was accomplished in either case, you formed thoughts upside down, and your mind ran on lewdness without end, so that the field of your heart grew daily darker and your name and rank were all dissolved; therefore you are punished by the removal of your name. Yongzhen wept. He mended his ways and set himself to do good, and printed warnings against lust to wake the world. In the next examination he still took first place among the graduates, and rose to be a provincial judge.

Li Deng at eighteen took first place in the provincial recommendation. After that he failed until he was fifty. He went to Master Ye Jing, the Dharma Master, to ask the reason. The master questioned Emperor Wen, who ordered a clerk to bring the register and show it. Li Deng had been granted a jade seal at birth: at eighteen he was to be first among the graduates, at nineteen the chief graduate, and at fifty-two to reach the office of Right Chancellor. Because after he passed he peeped at a neighbour's daughter bathing, he was delayed ten years and set down two grades. Because he encroached on the house-site of his elder brother Li Feng, he was delayed another ten years and set down three grades. Because he violated a decent woman of the Zheng family, he was delayed another ten years. And now he had again violated a maiden of his neighbours. Since he did not mend his evil, his name had been erased, and he would fail all his life. The master told Deng, and Deng died of shame and remorse. Alas. How many years had his forefathers accumulated virtue for him to obtain the chief graduate's place and the chancellorship, and he cut it away like this, betraying the grace of Heaven and betraying his ancestors. And the joy and power of it: compared with the degree, it is not one part in ten thousand. Yet for a little lewdness and arrogance he lost a great deal of blessing and emolument. How sad. Yu Tieqiao said: The chief graduate and the chancellorship are not hard to wipe out with one stroke of the brush — how much more so for those below them. I secretly fear for them without end.

Liu Guan of Longshu had a son, Yaoju, whose courtesy name was Tangqing. He hired a boat to go to the examination. The boatman had a daughter, and Yaoju made advances to her, but the boatman kept watch and ward so strictly that he could not come near. On the day of the examination, the boatman thought that within the barred and thorn-hedged precincts there was nothing to fear, and went into the market to trade. Now the examination questions happened to be ones Yaoju had prepared privately, so he came out of the hall very early. The boatman had not returned, and in the end he had commerce with the girl. One evening Liu Guan and his wife dreamed that two men in yellow came galloping up to announce the roll, saying: Your son is first on the list. Guan wished to see the roll, but a man beside him suddenly snatched it away, saying: Liu Yaoju has lately done a deceitful thing and has already received the punishment of Heaven. When the names were filled in, he was indeed rejected for a trifling fault, and in the end he died without passing.

In the Jiajing era of the Ming there was Lu Zhongxi, who was born with uncommon talent. At seventeen he lived in the capital with his teacher, a certain Qiu. Opposite their door was a girl of great beauty, and master and pupil peeped at her again and again and were stirred. The teacher said: The City God is the most powerful. Go and pray, and perhaps there may be a match. So he prayed. That night both dreamed that they were pursued by the City God, who rebuked them sharply, saying: What manner of wretches are you, to darken your hearts and profane the god in this way? He ordered an inquiry into their emolument and rank. The clerk searched the register. Under Lu's name was written: Chief graduate in the jiaxu year. Under Qiu's name there was nothing at all. The god said: As for Lu, I shall report to the Most High and erase his roll of emolument, and make him poor and lowly all his life. As for Qiu, pull out his intestines. The dream had scarcely ended when Qiu died of colic. Zhongxi afterwards was poor and lowly all his life, as the god had said.

Li Yan, Censor of the Tang, was on a mission to Lingbiao when he suddenly met a tiger that had gone into the thicket and spoke in human speech, saying: I nearly hurt you. You are my old friend. Yan said: How like the voice of Li Wei, my fellow graduate. The tiger said: It is long since we parted. He spoke of their old friendship in full detail. Yan asked how he had come to this. He said: One day as I sat in quiet, I suddenly heard a voice calling outside the door, and I went mad, and came to this shape. Now that I see an old friend, can I be without grief? Yan asked whether he had any regret left in his life. He said: I once violated a widow outside the walls of Nanyang. Her family found it out and secretly plotted to harm me, and I, being drunk, wiped out the whole household. That is enough for regret. Then he gave a great roar and went off.

In Jingxi there were two men who were friends from the time their hair hung loose. When they grew up, one was rich and one poor. The poor man's wife was beautiful. The rich man laid a scheme, saying there was a wealthy house where they might find a living. The poor man thanked him. The rich man provided the boat and carried the wife along with them. As they neared a mountain, he said: Leave your wife to watch the boat; you and I will go on ahead. He led him into the forest, drew the hatchet from his belt, and cut him dead. Then he came down the mountain pretending to weep, and said to the wife: Your husband has died by a tiger. The woman wept bitterly. The rich man said: Let me go with you and search for him. Together they went up the mountain, and when they came to a quiet place in the glen, he embraced her and demanded lewdness. The woman screamed aloud. Suddenly a tiger came out of the thicket and carried the rich man off. The woman fled in terror, thinking her husband had indeed fallen into the tiger's mouth, and weeping, went back. Far off she saw a man weeping as he came through the hills: it was her husband. They took each other's hands and wept aloud, and when each had told the tale, the husband said: He schemed to violate you, but you were not violated; he schemed to kill me, but I am not dead. What have I to resent? The wife said: I grieved that you were dead, but you are not dead; I wished to repay the villain, but the villain has repaid himself. What have I to resent? So their grief turned to joy, and they went home to their village.

Wang Qinzheng of Chuyang had an intrigue with a neighbour's wife, and there was a pact between them to run away together. Fearing that her husband would overtake them, the woman plotted to kill him. When Zheng heard of it he was greatly terrified, and at once fled alone to Jiangshan County, seventy li away. He thought himself far enough, and that he might escape the calamity. Hungry, he entered an eating-house. The innkeeper set out food for two. Zheng asked the reason. He said: Just now a man with unbound hair followed you in. Is that not two? Zheng knew that an aggrieved ghost was following him, and so he went to the authorities and gave himself up. Both the man and the woman were executed according to law.

In the Jiajing era of the Ming there was a widow of a dye-house in Yixing, Madame Chen, who had beauty. A timber merchant saw her and desired her. On the pretext of dyeing he came often to her house, and enticed her in a hundred ways. When he knew she could not be moved, he threw several timbers into her house, and next day informed the authorities that she had stolen them; and he bribed the clerks and runners to bind and humiliate her, hoping she would yield. Day and night the woman prayed pitifully before the Altar of the Dark, saying: My house has reverently sacrificed to the gods longer than any; can you not protect me? That night she dreamed that the god said: I have already commanded the black tiger. The timber merchant heard of it and still reviled her as a foolish woman. Not many days later he went into the mountains with six or seven men to buy timber. A tiger came out of the forest, passed by several men, and carried off his head in its jaws.

A certain licentiate Guo of Jiangning entered the examination hall in the jimao year. Before the roll was posted, a certain Mr. Yang, who lived opposite, said to him: I have lately become a judge in the courts of the underworld, and I know that you should pass in the fifty-seventh place. But on a certain day of a certain month, when you were collecting rent in Jiangbei, you had illicit commerce with a farmer's wife under the stars and moon; and a maidservant in your house was taken by you and died of ill treatment, and she has come again and again to lodge her complaint, and though I pleaded hard for you, that woman's resentment cannot be dissolved. For this your name has been struck from the roll.

Zhang Bao was prefect of Chengdu. There was the wife of Lieutenant Li of Huayang, whose beauty was the finest in Shu, and Bao wished to have her secretly. He begged nuns and wet nurses on every side to convey his meaning privately, and in time the wife's heart was also moved; and it happened that Lieutenant Li was ruined by a charge of corruption, and Bao impeached him, and he was sent to prison for full examination and banished beyond the passes, where he died on the road. Bao then bribed the lieutenant's mother richly and took the woman by force, and gave himself up to joy without ceasing. Before long the woman fell ill and was dazed, and saw Lieutenant Li standing beside her. At the point of death she said to Bao: I am grateful for your kindness, and dare not fail to repay it. The lieutenant has already complained to Heaven, and will take you within a day. If you stay deep within your house you may not give him his chance; but if you go out lightly, you will surely be seized. Having spoken, she died. Not long after, Bao too fell ill. Mindful of the woman's words, he kept guard over himself very strictly and did not dare set foot outside his door. One day, sitting at dusk, he saw far off among the bamboos below the hall a red sleeve beckoning lightly. Thinking it was the lieutenant's wife, he hurried to her with all speed: it was the lieutenant. He seized him and beat him savagely, and cursed him, saying: You thieving wretch, if the red sleeve had not waved, would you have come? After a long while blood flowed from his nose, and he told his household the reason, and died.

Yan Wu of the Tang, when young, lived next door to an army commissioner and enticed his daughter to run away with him. The commissioner went to the palace and lodged a complaint, and an edict was issued for their arrest. Wu, fearing the penalty, killed the girl and sank her in the water, and so, as she was not found, he escaped by luck. Afterwards, when he was in Shu, he fell ill, and saw the girl before him, rebuking him, saying: That I went with you was indeed a failure of conduct; yet I in truth never wronged you. Even if you feared the penalty, why did you not let me go? To go so far as to kill me — you are truly a man without feeling. I have already complained in the courts of the underworld, and the day is fixed for tomorrow. Wu, ashamed and afraid, begged for his life. At dawn he died. Alas. At such a moment all the authority of a military governor availed him not a hair. Men today are always in haste to seek death; how should they know that after death kindness turns to enmity, and enmity never ends?

Xu Zhaoxin of Jinjiang in the Ming was a graduate of the wuwu year. He went to Funing Prefecture to call on the examiner of his own hall, and chanced to pass a nunnery, where he took a liking to a young nun and coerced her by his power and violated her. The next day he bit his tongue into two pieces and died. Again, Wang Wu of Jinjiang had a name for letters. He brought wine and drank in the Chengtian Temple, entered the hall of the canon, and saw a young novice sitting upright reading the sutras. He forced him to drink; the novice would not. He then embraced and fondled him. Three days after he went home, he suddenly slapped his own mouth and reviled himself, and bit his tongue until the blood flowed over the ground, and died. The death of these two was but the flower-retribution; the fruit lies in hell.

An old man of Jiangxi once lodged in a woman's house and committed lewdness with one of her kin, and a child was born secretly and buried. Afterwards his house grew fairly prosperous, and he enjoyed it for a long time. Those who knew the matter said the way of Heaven was not to be questioned. Later his son and grandson had an intrigue with a servant, and the old man, seeing it, was enraged. He took a coffin, and nailed the two of them into it alive. Lawsuits dragged on for years, and his property was exhausted, and he died.

Mr. Shen was by nature strong and vigorous, and he repeatedly committed adultery. Wang Xing'an once warned him, saying: “If I violate another man's wife, another man will violate mine. The retribution is fearsome. You would do well to mend your ways a little.” Shen laughed and said: “Have you ever seen a man fond of beauty become a cuckold? I keep my women's quarters strictly shut; what is there to worry about?” One day he came home from outside and saw with his own eyes his wife coupling naked with another man. He wanted to seize a weapon and strike them, but his hand could not be raised. His wife, thinking her husband would not make an issue of it, took her pleasure with the man at leisure. Shen, in a fury, glared, stamped his feet, heaved one deep sigh, and died.

A certain man had done evil all his life. One close to him was lodging in his house by night when he heard two voices speaking: “So-and-so's wickedness is full to overflowing; he must receive retribution.” One asked, “Shall he have his line cut off?” The answer came, “Too heavy.” “Shall he suffer fire?” “Too light.” “Wang Xiaoxiao.” “Enough, enough.” The hearer was astonished and could not make out the reason. Some years later the man became infatuated with a courtesan, this Wang Xiaoxiao, and married her and brought her home. He listened to her words and followed her counsel; she estranged his own flesh and blood, and when his wealth was utterly exhausted, he died.

The monk Xingyun saw a lotus blossom sway and suddenly gave rise to a lustful thought. That night a woman knocked at his door. Xingyun opened it and saw a maiden with a maidservant, who called herself Lady Lotus, her face and figure bright enough to dazzle a man. Xingyun was overjoyed and dallied and talked with her. In a moment the lamp went out. The attendant heard Xingyun crying out in pain. The woman said in a stern voice: “Why did you rashly give rise to a lustful heart? Even if I were truly a woman, would I be willing to lie with you illicitly?” The attendant ran to tell the monks, and they pushed open the door and entered. What they saw was two yakṣas. Xingyun's head was already parted from his body.

This compilation sets out one after another the cases of calamity brought by lust, and it places the case of the scholar of Guixi first precisely in order to make plain the subtle meaning of the Most High's words, “when the thought arises, it is a private act”: to urge men to be cautious and reverent at the very beginning, in the moment when the eye sees and the mind stirs, and to take pains to be careful there. And this case of Xingyun is not even a matter of the mind stirring at the sight of beauty; it is without head or brain, the mind conjuring up images, building a tower where there is no mirage, holding a market where there is no sea, secretly and darkly fashioning evil, boring its own chaos open — until at last the yakṣas devour him and his head is parted from his body. Wicked demons and monstrous calamities, cruel and ghastly to this degree. Reading this case, who would not tremble in heart and shudder in liver? Therefore I make it the conclusion; there is deep meaning in this. Think on it, think on it.

Lin Maoxian of Xinzhou was a man of great talent, and he was recommended for the provincial examination. His family was poor, so he shut his door and studied. A neighbor girl, whose own husband did not study, admired Maoxian's fame for talent and came to him by night. Maoxian rebuked her, saying: “Man and woman must keep their separate places; the rites and the law do not permit it. Heaven and earth, the gods and the spirits, are ranged and spread all around us. How could you defile me?” The girl withdrew in shame. The next year Maoxian passed the examination, and afterward all three of his sons passed as well.

Yao Sanjiu was originally surnamed Bian, a man of wide learning and skilled in poetry and prose, and he taught in the house of the Huai family. A daughter of the house often came spying on him; Bian sat stern and upright and paid her no heed. One day he set his shoes out to dry in the courtyard, and the girl wrote a letter and slipped it into his shoe. Bian found it and made some other excuse to take his leave and go home. Yuan Yixing wrote a poem in praise of him, with the lines: “One speck of chastity, firm as no stone; / let not the spring wind and peach and plum suspect each other.” Bian would not accept the poem, and moreover answered with a letter insisting that there had been no such thing. Yixing sealed up his letter and wrote on it: “Virtue is most abundant; his sons and grandsons will surely flourish.” Later his son Chen and his great-grandson Xi both passed the imperial examination.

In his youth Tang Gao was reading by his lamp when a woman teased him and poked a hole through the paper window. Tang Gao mended it and wrote a poem on it, saying: “A paper window poked through is easy to mend; / it is hardest to repair the hidden virtue one has harmed.” One evening a monk passed his gate and saw a plaque reading “Number One Scholar,” with two lanterns hung to left and right, and on them were just these two lines. Astonished, the monk questioned him about it. In the end he indeed came first in the whole empire.

Wang Tianyu met a man of strange powers who read his face and said: “Your features resemble those of an arhat, but you will lack heirs, and your life will not be long.” Thereupon Wang made light of wealth and delighted in giving. One day, lodging at Qingjiangpu, his young and pretty hostess came to him of her own accord. Wang shut the door and would not admit her, saying: “How could I ruin your reputation and your chastity?” The woman went away ashamed. Later he met the physiognomist again, who said: “What hidden virtue have you done? Your features have suddenly changed. You ought to have a noble son, and to live past eighty.” In the end it was as he said. Looking over the sages of old who turned away women who came running to them, some drew their strength from the word “forbearance” — “what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.” Some feared to damage their hidden merit, dreading only that their blessings would be cut short and their years shortened. Their learning may have differed, yet all alike accorded with the uprightness of heavenly principle and the peace of the human heart; it is the way by which both self and other are kept whole. At such a moment, when blessing comes, the mind grows quick: one already seems to have climbed serenely into the blue clouds, and does not wait for the reward before rejoicing. In sum, the ways of turning away women who come running are not one; one must know them all in advance in careful detail, and only then will one not be confused when the matter arrives. There are many, indeed, who by a stern countenance and a sharp rebuke send her away at once. But there are also those who refuse and she still will not go, like Lu Rong, who pleaded that his illness was not yet healed and agreed to a meeting a few nights later — both are fit models. Or one may open the door and go out: thus Cao Fen went to lodge elsewhere, the quick response of a man of complete virtue. There are also those who swear to die: thus Mao Lumen refused the maidservant who came running to him, and when she said, “If so, then I have only death,” Lumen was not moved. There are those who refuse her all night and she is still there, like Doctor Chen — “I cannot, I cannot” — who then pushed open the window and stood exposed in the courtyard, vowing to do nothing base. And there is the man who firmly declined a gift of a hundred pieces of gold and still refused her sternly — such pure virtue and resolute decision is truly fit to be a model. If the door is already shut and the woman is outside, the door must not be opened. If in the morning one makes an excuse and takes leave to go home and she still summons one, one must not come again. Yet one must never speak of it in all one's life; even one's wife and children should not be told of the matter. Only this is abundant virtue. From this one ascends to be first in the empire, attains high position, brings glory to one's forebears, and prolongs one's line. Compared with piling up merit along other roads, the difference in difficulty is ten thousand times over.

In Zhejiang there was a certain commandant who engaged a tutor to instruct his son. The tutor fell ill with a cold and wished to bring on a sweat, so he had the boy fetch him a quilt. By mistake the boy rolled up one of his mother's shoes in it. When the illness was over and the quilt was returned, the shoe fell out beside the mat; neither the tutor nor the boy knew of it. The commandant saw it and suspected his wife of an intrigue. She would not submit, so he sent a maidservant to invite the tutor in his wife's name by a ruse. The tutor angrily rebuked the maid. The commandant then forced his wife to go in person, while he himself held a bare blade and waited for the door to open. The tutor firmly refused, saying: “I was invited here by my host; how could I fall into secret misconduct? I swear I will never open this door.” In the morning the tutor took his leave. The commandant said: “Sir, you are truly a gentleman,” and told him the whole story and begged him to stay. That examination season the tutor passed.

Cheng Yanbin attacked the city of Ning. On the day the city fell, his attendants presented him with three virgins, all of uncommon beauty. He was drunk at the time, and said to the girls: “You are as my own daughters; how would I dare violate you?” He sealed them into a room by himself, and at dawn he sought out their parents and returned them. Afterward he rose to the office of inspector, and at the age of ninety-three he took leave of family and friends and passed away. All his sons became eminent.

Xu Xi of Jiangyin in the Ming dynasty was, when he was a clerk in the military office, involved in a case where men were taken for garrison duty in distant lands and a strong man was drafted. By mistake this fell upon one man, who could not clear himself and wished to beg Xu Xi to release him. His family was poor, but his wife was young and beautiful, so he set out wine for Xu Xi and had his wife drink with him. Presently the man made an excuse and left. Xu Xi hurried out, but the wife, afraid that Xu Xi would go and ruin the matter, caught at his robe to keep him and told him her husband's intention. Xu Xi refused her sternly, tore his robe free, and fled. The next day he reproved her husband severely, and in the end cleared him. Afterward Xu Xi rose in office to be Minister of War.

Zhang Wenqi of Fujian and a certain Zhou fled from bandits into a mountain cave. A beautiful woman was already there before them. Seeing the men arrive, she fled in panic. Zhang said: “If you go, you will surely meet the bandits. We are honest and careful men; we too have come here to escape the bandits, and would never dare violate you.” In the middle of the night Zhou repeatedly tried to assault her, and Zhang restrained him with all his strength. At dawn Zhang and Zhou left the cave to look for news, meaning to draw Zhou out with him and leave the woman in peace. Once out of the mountains they learned the bandits had withdrawn, so they came back to the cave with a village elder, who asked after the woman's parents, her native place, and her surname. Zhang urgently had the elder escort her home. Not long after, a certain Mr. Huang prepared a generous dowry and took Zhang as his son-in-law: it was the woman who had taken refuge from the bandits. Her father, moved by Zhang's virtue, gave her to him in marriage. Afterward both of Zhang's sons passed the examinations.

Mr. Chen of Yugan was skilled in medicine. A poor scholar fell ill with a wasting disease and was near death; Chen treated him and cured him, and did not demand payment. Later Chen passed by his house at dusk and was pressed to stay the night. The mother-in-law said to her daughter-in-law: “Your husband owes his life to that man. Why do you not share his bed to repay him?” The wife murmured assent. That night she came to him. Chen refused her, saying: “What of your mother-in-law?” The wife said: “This was my mother-in-law's own wish.” He said: “What of your husband?” She said: “My husband's body was your gift; what claim has he on me?” Chen said: “I cannot.” She pressed him, and Chen said again and again: “I cannot, I cannot.” So he sat until dawn, and taking up a brush wrote the words “I cannot” over and over on the desk. Afterward, when he could barely hold himself in check, he cried out aloud: “These two words, I cannot — they are very hard.” Then he pushed open the window and stood exposed in the courtyard, and went away only at daybreak. Later, when Chen's son entered the examinations, the chief examiner threw out his paper. Suddenly he heard a voice call: “You cannot.” He read it again and again threw it out, and again heard the voice cry repeatedly: “You cannot, you cannot.” The last time he read it, he had resolved to throw it out, when suddenly he heard a loud voice cry: “These two words, I cannot — they are very hard,” and the cry would not stop. The examiner therefore passed him, and afterward he became a presented scholar. All the above are cases of a heart set on uprightness and free of private desire. But there is no way to deal with one in whom principle and desire are locked in battle. So I set out this case of one who held firm on the verge of chaos, to show the method.

Qi Wang of Jinhua was fifty and had no son. A physiognomist said: “You have an evil air about you; you must have something on your conscience.” Qi Wang said: “In my youth I once violated a woman in her inner chamber.” The physiognomist said in alarm: “For that offense a man's sons and grandsons ought to be cut off. Of all evils, lust is the hardest to repent. Some great good is needed before Heaven's mind can be turned back.” Qi Wang therefore reformed. In the first year, he rejoiced in giving and was never stingy when men proposed good works. The physiognomist said: “Not yet.” In the second year, whenever he met with a good work hard to perform, he was first to contribute more than half. The physiognomist said: “Not yet.” In the third year, he carried out good works single-handed and would not yield precedence to others. The physiognomist said: “The lines of hidden merit have appeared; why worry that you will have no son?” In the end he had a son. At seventy Qi Wang was still able to hold his grandson in his arms.

Lu Qing of the Ming dynasty loved to talk of lewdness and to peep at women. At thirty he was utterly poor, and two sons died one after the other. One day he suddenly died, and saw his grandfather, who said in anger: “Our two generations piled up goodness; the retribution due you was a vast fortune. Who would have thought your heart would love lust and your mouth and eyes create sin, so that your blessings were all but cut away? I feared you would again commit the actual evil of lust, and that your descendants would be utterly without hope, so I earnestly begged the King of the Underworld to summon you here for a look, that you might know the gain and loss.” Lu Qing said: “I have heard that violating another man's wife or daughter brings the retribution of no descendants, and I truly feared that; I never committed it.” An official beside them said: “Is it only the cutting off of descendants? If a woman comes to seduce you and you do not refuse her, then you are only repaid with no descendants. But as for those who lure and coerce, and those who offend again and again, those who ruin relations, those who procure abortions, those who kill husbands — what crimes are those? Is it only the cutting off of descendants? The yang law is lenient toward lustful evil; the yin law is strictest of all. Whenever a man stirs a single thought of desire, the three corpse-spirits report it of themselves, and the Kitchen God and the City God petition on high; to conceal or omit any part of it is a grave fault. Only watch today's sentencing and you will know.” In a little while the ghost attendants brought in a crowd of lustful offenders, cangue-laden and kneeling. The King of the Underworld gave his orders in a stern voice, saying: “So-and-so is to become a beggar, mad and mute. So-and-so is to become a prostitute, blind. So-and-so is to be an ox for two lives. So-and-so is to be a pig for ten lives.” All were led out by the ghost attendants to be reborn. Lu Qing's hair stood on end and his marrow froze. The official said: “There are things worse even than these. Do not covet half a moment of pleasure and lose this human body. You should shun beauty as you would an arrow, and carve these words to admonish the world.” Afterward the King of the Underworld released Lu Qing to return. Lu Qing carved and printed the Record of a Journey Through the Underworld, printing ten thousand copies to awaken the world. He did good with all his strength. At forty he had two sons in succession and raised a fortune of ten thousand in gold. Then he cut off all worldly ties and went to the Southern Sea to cultivate the Way. Cai Jing, a man of his own village, wrote it down. The two cases above, the good reward of repentance for lust, are set out here in order to make firm the repentant heart of those who have already stumbled. For this is the way to turn calamity into blessing. Alas! The one evil of lust — the brush can hardly exhaust it, and how could speech ever come to its end? I can only daily hope that the wise and the foolish, those who have not yet offended and those already stained, will each and all think deeply on it, and that their heavenly conscience may come to light early.

Goods are vessels and implements; wealth is silver and money; to be in debt means to have borrowed them in a time of need to tide oneself over, and then, after a long while, to be ungrateful and not repay. The Scripture of Admonitions says: “If you owe another a debt and for the moment have nothing with which to make it good, think long and anxiously of the debt, and diligently consider how to repay it.” If because one has not repaid it, one instead wishes that the creditor might die and so wipe out the trace of it, such a mind as this is a jackal and a wolf in this present life, and how could it escape becoming dog or horse in the life to come? It is foolishness indeed.

Bai Yuantong owed Yang Yun four thousand five hundred cash and, though pressed again and again, did not repay it. When Yang Yun died, he simply concealed the matter. Later the Yang family had a donkey born to them, which suddenly spoke in human speech, saying: “I am Bai Yuantong. Because I owed you four thousand five hundred cash, I have come to this. Now the donkey-selling family in the Western Market likewise owes money to me, exactly this sum. Sell me to them quickly, and take the price to repay yourselves, and the debt will be settled.” Yang's son did as he said; two days after the sale the donkey died.

Yan Chang of the Han dynasty was a commandery officer. The governor Diwu Chang was once summoned to court, and entrusted to Yan Chang a hundred and thirty thousand cash of his salary, which Yan Chang buried. Later, when Diwu Chang was dying, he summoned his orphaned grandson of nine and said to him: “I have thirty thousand cash left with the officer Yan Chang.” When the grandson grew up he sought out Yan Chang, who was both grieved and glad to see him, and at once took out the money and returned it, the seals and markings just as they had been. The grandson said: “My grandfather said only thirty thousand; now it is a hundred and thirty thousand. I dare not take it.” Yan Chang said: “The governor, sick and confused, spoke in error. Have no doubt, young sir.” In the end he returned it all. Yan Chang afterward rose to be provincial governor.

To solicit means every matter great and small; whoever begs or entreats or asks a favor of another, all of it is this. Not to succeed means not to get one's wish. To curse is to wish calamity upon him; to hate is to store up resentment and venom. The noble man understands principle and rests content in his lot; how could he be willing to solicit from others? If perchance he does so, he is already no upright man. And if he does not succeed, he should only turn and examine himself. If he goes further and curses and hates, then he is truly a petty man who turns and turns again.

In the Song dynasty a certain Lu went by night carrying a hundred pieces of gold to Wang Dan, asking to be made transport commissioner for the Huai and Yangtze region. The duke declined, saying: “Your talents are not equal to this office. How would I dare set public matters aside for private favor?” Lu withdrew in shame, and all night long burned incense and cursed, wishing Wang Dan a speedy death. In a dream a god rebuked him, saying: “Wang is loyal in heart to the state, and you wish him a speedy death. The Emperor of Heaven will bring the guilt home to you.” Indeed, within a few days Lu died.

Li Geng of Hangzhou in the Ming dynasty was poor and of no principle. From all his relatives and neighbors he went about begging loans, and if he met the least refusal he fell into unending rage and hatred. One day he asked a friend for grain, and when the friend would not consent, Li Geng at once cursed him before the god, wishing him a speedy death. In a moment there was a crash of thunder, and Li Geng fell dead before the god.

Yu Tieqiao said: In soliciting from others, my own feelings may be most urgent, but of the men from whom one solicits, some are without the means and some are constrained by circumstance, so that nine in ten appeals fail and one in ten succeeds. This is the ordinary way of things. If one rashly gives rise to curses and hatred, will the other man, because of my curses and hatred, suddenly turn about and pity me? One only adds to the obstruction of one's own afflictions. Such a man not only does not know the decree of Heaven; he also does not understand the ways of the world.

Xie Liangzuo of the Song dynasty said: In all things there is in truth a decree; human calculation cannot contend with it. In all my life I have never solicited from others, and my letters have never reached those in power. When someone urged me to do so, I answered: “How could he promote me? I have my own decree.” Fan Zhongxuan of the Song dynasty said: “Though a man be utterly foolish, in reproving others he is clear-sighted; though a man be utterly clear-sighted, in forgiving himself he is blind. If a man can reprove himself with the heart with which he reproves others, and forgive others with the heart with which he forgives himself, the station of sage and worthy — there is no fear he will not reach it.” Whoever solicits from others and lays blame on them should repeat these two gentlemen's words three times over.

To lose one's opportunity means to meet with a matter that cannot be done and to find oneself in circumstances where one cannot get one's way. In the affairs and circumstances of this world, ruin is easy and success is hard, and the adverse outnumber the favorable. One may have an unlucky fate and an unpropitious time, so that whatever one does is thrown into confusion; or one may by a chance error go wrong and find it too late to repent. The hardship of the road is the same lament in every age. Yet there is a kind of man who is not near to human feeling: in ordinary days he loves to make a show of friendship, but once trouble and defeat come he always places himself outside the game and laughs at the man whose elbows are being pulled, saying: “It was his own fault in the first place.” Alas! Let him examine his own life in turn: has he truly never once done a single thing amiss?

Wang Sheng of Hanzhou in the Ming dynasty loved to point out other men's faults. A neighbor of his had lost a son, and Wang Sheng upbraided him, saying: “It is because your wickedness is extreme that you have this retribution.” Not long after, Wang Sheng's own two sons both died of illness, and the neighbor mocked him in turn, saying: “I suppose your wickedness must be even more extreme.” Again, when a cousin of his clan sat for the annual examination and was placed in the fourth rank, Wang Sheng pointed at him too, saying: “His writing is truly absurd; how could he hope for a high place?” Within a year, in the provincial examination Wang Sheng himself was placed in the fifth rank, and his cousin mocked him in turn, saying: “I suppose my cousin's writing is even more absurd.”

Guan Zhong said: “I once planned affairs together with Bao Shu, and instead met with deeper poverty and hardship; Bao Shu did not think me foolish, knowing that time may be favorable or unfavorable. I was three times an official and three times driven out by my lord; Bao Shu did not think me unworthy, knowing that I had not met my time.” From this we may see that the great men of old, too, often had their lost opportunities. What is precious is a man who understands one, to comfort and encourage one in the midst of poverty and hardship. How could one, because his steps have once gone astray, go on to drop stones upon him? Such a man has lost the duty of compassion and has turned his back on the benevolence of lending a hand; he delights in calamity and rejoices in disaster, and is neither benevolent nor wise. Calamity will surely overtake his own person.

A body maimed in its four limbs, a form and feature coarse and mean — these come either from evil karma in a former life or from the misfortunes visited upon one by one's parents. When one meets such people, one ought to pity them and keep them whole; how could one bear to mock them? And moreover a man's accomplishment lies in his capacity and discernment, not in his bodily form. Zhou Bo, though he stammered, became a minister; Yan Ying, though small of body, brought his lord to prominence. These are recorded in the histories and cannot be numbered. And since men whose bodies are incomplete often hate themselves for it, to mock them is to tread upon what they most resent. The mother of Duke Qing of Qi laughed at Que Ke and was attacked. The beauty of the Lord of Pingyuan laughed at a lame man and was put to death. The people of Zhao mocked Lord Mengchang as a little man and were killed. All these are overturned carts before us, and may serve as deep warnings.

The Buddhist scriptures speak of the fruit that flows on evenly from like to like, meaning that when a man lives in the world with a mind and craft not upright, then in life after life to come his bodily form will be incomplete, his mouth and eyes askew, his four limbs maimed and lacking. This says that karma made in a former life is the cause of the incomplete body and form one receives in this life. If so, then when a man is at the very point of giving rise to a thought, in the subtle stirring of a single motion of mind, may he not be warned, cautious, and in fear, lest he drift into what is crooked and perverse?

The Essential Summary of the Daoist Canon says: The prohibitions concerning the bedchamber are many, and those concerning thunder are the most severe of all. The Monthly Ordinances says: Three days before the first thunder, the wooden clapper is sounded to proclaim to the myriad people: “Thunder is about to sound. Those who do not keep watch over their bearing and conduct will bear children incomplete, and calamity will surely follow.” This is because they profane the majesty of Heaven. Here it speaks of parents who are not careful, and so bring it about that their children's bodies are incomplete.

Lu Qi of the Tang dynasty had a face the color of indigo. When Guo Ziyi fell ill, the hundred officials came in throngs to inquire after him, and his concubines and attendants filled the room before him, nor did he ever send them out. But when Lu Qi arrived, he had them all withdrawn. Someone asked him why, and Guo Ziyi said: “His face is ugly and his heart is treacherous. If the women see him they will surely laugh, and one day when he gains power, not one of my clan will be left alive.” Later Lu Qi became prime minister, and took revenge for the smallest glance; only the Guo family alone came through unscathed.

Hou Yuan'gong was very poor in appearance. When he first drank at the provincial banquet, men did not respect him because he was advanced in years and ugly. Some frivolous fellows painted Yuan'gong's likeness on a paper kite and let it fly on a string. Yuan'gong saw it and laughed, and wrote on it: “Unmet, in hiding, who would trust my worth? / Only now my name and trace appear. / For no cause the skillful craftsman paints my form; / I borrow the wind lightly, and with one lift mount the empty sky. / Barely does the breeze lift me and my body steady grows; / I almost doubt I journey far to the moon palace. / After the rain the evening sun is red. / How many men on level ground / Look up and see me among the purple clouds?” That year he passed the examination and rose to the office of prime minister. The boys of his home village were all too ashamed to face him.

Yu Tieqiao said: A man's body and form are by nature nothing to rely on. The crippled, the sick, the maimed, the disabled — none of these can be known in advance. A beautiful eye may be pierced and blinded; a swift foot may be broken and lamed. “From now on I know how to escape this” — how fraught with peril were those words of Zengzi! If one has not even time enough to love oneself, how dare one laugh at others? Those who make up nicknames, compose songs and rhymes, and sketch and mock at others — let them take this to heart and change their evil habits once for all.

To suppress talent at the sight of it is not the same as hiding the good and thwarting the excellent. Hiding carries the meaning of dark confinement; thwarting carries the misery of breaking and snapping. This goes a step further still. For to withhold praise where praise is due is precisely to suppress. Compared with the two preceding articles, the guilt seems somewhat lighter, yet the scrutiny is all the finer.

In the Warring States period Li Si and Han Fei of Zhou both studied under Xun Qing. Li Si knew in his own heart that his ability was not the equal of Han Fei's. When the King of Qin read Han Fei's book The Difficulties of Persuasion, he lamented that he could not meet the man. Later, when the King of Han sent Han Fei on a mission to Qin, the King of Qin spoke with him and was greatly pleased. Li Si feared he would be favored, slandered him, and had him thrown into prison, sending him poison. Han Fei wished to plead his own case but was not permitted an audience, and so died. Later Li Si was slandered by Zhao Gao and likewise wished to plead his case, and was not permitted. Those who understood took it as Heaven's way of returning like for like.

Sun Bian of the Song dynasty was a man of Meishan. He and Tang Jie and Wu Zhongfu had not known one another at first, but he admired their firmness and uprightness and therefore recommended them with all his strength, and they were promoted to censors. Zhang Xungong and Wen Lugong had never met, but hearing of their forthrightness, he recommended them at first sight, and afterward they went out as generals and came home as ministers. Yang Jingzhi loved talent and was just in heart; he once came to know a scholar of Jiangbiao named Xiang Si, and presented him with a poem: “Everywhere I see your poems, and all your poems are good; / and when I look upon your character, it surpasses your poems. / All my life I have not understood how to hide another's excellence: / wherever I go I tell everyone of Xiang Si.” These several gentlemen all advanced men of their own kind and encouraged and rewarded talent. Those who cannot seek out worthies for the state not only obstruct and suppress those who come after; they also cut off the seed by which the hundred families might be blessed. Alas! If one knows that to know men is the height of benevolence, then one knows that to envy the worthy is great evil.

According to the Code of the Mystic Capital, when offenses accumulate to two thousand seven hundred, that is one harm, and the family ought to produce a male or female shaman. If so, then to be born a shaman is already to be a man who made karma in a former age, and now to bury effigies and cast spells to harm others on another's behalf is only to deepen one's own hell. But there are those who give rise to the thought and have another do it; their guilt is even graver than the shaman's. If there be such, the king's law ought to behead them, and the yin law is stricter still.

Gongsun Chao, registrar of Wangwu in the Tang dynasty, died suddenly upon taking office. One day he appeared in a dream to the county magistrate and said: “I have a grievance and beg Your Honor to redress it. My allotted span was not yet due to end; I was killed by sorcery by my servants and concubines so that they might steal from me. My home is at Heyin. If Your Honor will secretly choose able officers and go with a warrant to arrest them, not one will slip the net. Under the eastern end of the hall's eaves, beneath the seventh roof-tile, there is a likeness of me made of tung wood, with nails driven all over it; it has already begun to change. The next day the magistrate did choose strong soldiers, took the warrant, and sent a letter to the magistrate of Heyin. They seized all the servants and concubines and searched beneath the hall's eaves. They found a human figure more than a foot long, its whole body covered with nails, the wood gradually turning to flesh; when struck it gave out a dull sound. All the grain and wheat Gongsun Chao had gathered had been stolen away. The magistrate then reported the matter to the prefecture, and all were executed. Now sorcery and baleful arts have their source mostly among women, maidservants, and concubines, for they wish to use them to grasp power and win favor, and their greed for gain is even more urgent than others'. People today should by all means set their own persons upright and keep their households in order, and guard well their doors, not allowing shamans and heterodox teachers to come and go. This is the way to stop it at the source. As for those in office, they too should issue strict orders for the search and arrest of such people, to cut off their traces. The merit of this is no small matter.

Every blade of grass and every tree is the living intent of the Creator. Gao Chai would not break a growing shoot, and Confucius praised him. The Buddha said that trees of many years are mostly dwelt in by ghosts and spirits, and must not be lightly felled; those who fell them often meet with calamity. If even to fell them is not permitted, how much less to kill them with poison?

Ru Yunqu of Taoyuan was venomous by nature. At odds with a neighbor, he secretly used poison to kill every one of the fruit trees the neighbor had planted. One day Ru came home from outside and in a daze saw lamplight flickering and soldiers in a crowded throng. He was bound by a crowd of attendants and dragged into the woods, where a god rebuked him, saying: “Trees and grasses are living things of Heaven above. How dare you take your anger out on them and kill them? It must be that your five organs are all out of balance.” He had the attendants cut open Ru's belly and take out his lungs and liver. Ru woke in terror and died of a pain in his heart and belly.

Chen Shi invited a geomancer to survey his ancestral grave. The man saw a great tree before the grave, planted at the edge of another family's plot, and took it for closing off the celestial heart; it must be removed, he said, if there was any hope of success in the examinations. He therefore urged Chen to buy fish and secretly pierce the tree with poison. Chen would not. He said: “Both families are seeking good fortune. And moreover it is a towering great tree; how could I bear to kill it?” Within a year the tree happened to be torn out by a great wind, and the celestial heart was suddenly clear. His son Chen Kui then passed the examinations in quick succession and became a censor.

This is different from being disrespectful to one's teacher. Disrespect is to be disrespectful without cause; this is to be angry and resentful because of correction and reproof. The way of the ancients in serving a teacher knew neither offense nor concealment: whatever teaching was given, one ought to receive it with an open heart and a gentle temper. How could one be angry and resentful? One who is angry and resentful must be a man of shallow virtue and no blessing.

Wang Huidao of the Ming dynasty was by nature quick and discerning; a book once passed before his eyes and he could recite it, and at eight he could write compositions. But in serving his teacher he was exceedingly arrogant. At the least thing that crossed his wishes he would turn his back on his teacher and curse him in anger. One day, sitting alone in his study, he suddenly yawned, and out of his mouth leaped a ghost, who pointed at Dao and said: “You were meant to come first in the whole empire. Because you are angry and resentful toward your teacher, the High God has struck your name from the register of emolument, and I too am leaving you from this moment.” With these words it vanished. When he sought out his old pages, he was utterly blank and could not recognize a single character.

Wei Zhao of the Eastern Han dynasty, as a boy, met Guo Linzong. He considered that a teacher of texts is easy to find, but a teacher of men is hard to meet, and so he begged to attend upon him, fetching water and sweeping. Linzong once fell ill and told Zhao to make gruel. When the gruel was ready Zhao brought it in, and Linzong cried out at him: “Making gruel for an elder, and you do not attend to it with care and respect, so that it cannot be eaten!” Zhao made the gruel again and brought it once more, and three times more he was shouted at, yet Zhao's countenance never changed. Linzong said: “At first I saw your face; from this day on I know your heart.”

Deng Zhi of the Song dynasty was a village schoolmaster, skilled at drawing students on and guiding them. Words of filial piety and fraternal duty never left his lips. He met people with sincerity and taught and guided them with all his heart. In the reign of Shenzong his eldest son Wan became a Hanlin academician, and his second son Ji and two grandsons all passed the imperial examination in the same list. Men all said this was the recompense for Deng Zhi's wholehearted teaching and guidance. Now a child born into a family of warmth and plenty may have his temperament transformed in a single day; yet there are those in whom arrogance and indulgence have become second nature, who easily fall into delusion and idleness. All depends on the man who is their teacher to lead and guide them with skillful means and bring them to awakening. Strive at it, strive at it.

Contradiction and defiance is likewise not the same as secret insult. The evil of secret insult is deep; the guilt of contradiction is open. In every word and deed, the least trace of non-compliance is contradiction.
