Therefore he who can drink in measure — his wine is called the broth of great harmony, the friend that forgets feeling. He who cannot drink in measure — his wine is called the soft demon, the sweet poison.

Wine is the firewood of lust. To give free rein to wine and not to lust is rare indeed. When the inner fire is blazing and the desire of lust flares up, it is hard enough to guard against; how much more when one indulges in wine to feed that fire? To take a woman when drunk and full — the five viscera are overturned and the sickness is no small matter. This above all should be sternly punished. And there are those who, drunk, give rein to lust and so meet with insult and lose their lives; repentance then comes too late.

Nothing in the world is more laughable than contending for victory and defeat over the wine table. In dealing with the world, in every matter one should yield; how much more in a casual gathering for pleasure, where passing the drinking order and matching fists is no more than a moment's excitement. To win is no glory; to lose is no disgrace; to be beaten is no loss; to beat is no gain. It is exactly as the chess players say: victory is gladness indeed, but defeat may also be a joy. Yet these men are dull and know it not, and will not stop until they have won — until they are not drunk they will not cease. How extreme is their folly! And there are those who boast of their capacity and make it a grand deed that no one can match them, not knowing that in their own virtue, learning, and literary work, and in rank and fame, there is much in which they do not match others; yet they boast only of capacity. Is this not absurd? There is yet another kind, who take pride in the strictness of their drinking rules. They never think that wine is for making merry and should be taken according to each man's measure; why force others to drink much and so injure their lives? The saying goes: Tyrannical government is fiercer than a tiger. I say a tyrannical drinking rule is the same. If there be such a man at the table, one should hurry to withdraw from him.

In the Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom the failings of drinking are listed. They are: the mind knows no measure, one; wealth and goods are emptied out, two; the gate of many diseases, three; the root of strife, four; to go naked and barefoot, like cattle and horses, five; to dance wildly and curse at the table, hated and loathed by others, six; to fail to get what one ought to get, seven; to lose what one has got, eight; to tell out all one's secrets and repent when sober, nine; to make many mistakes in drink and feel shame when sober, ten; the body weak and strength soft, eleven; the complexion changing, twelve; the mind and will confused, thirteen; wisdom clouded, fourteen; not knowing to respect father and mother, fifteen; not knowing to respect the ghosts and gods, sixteen; not knowing to fear men's talk, seventeen; not knowing to fear the king's law, eighteen; factions and drunken violence, nineteen; estrangement from the worthy and good, twenty; no shame, twenty-one; quickness to rage, twenty-two; not keeping the six senses in check, twenty-three; giving free rein to lust without measure, twenty-four; being cast off by honorable men, twenty-five; having no careful caution or avoidance, twenty-six; making day into night so that all one's work is ruined, twenty-seven; committing offenses against the teachings of propriety, twenty-eight; casting away the good Dharma, twenty-nine; turning far from nirvāṇa, thirty; planting the cause of idiocy and madness, thirty-one; and at the breaking up of the body, at the end of life, falling into the evil paths, thirty-two. If one is again born a man, the mind is ever wild and disordered, and all outer goods and the means of living are utterly ruined.

A certain scholar Liu of Fujian was of strict and upright conduct and had very many pupils. In ordinary days he would always teach them to guard against lust. One day, having drunk by chance, he contended with a friend over a courtesan, and when he woke he repented greatly and was ashamed to face his students. He shut his door for three days and gathered all the cases, ancient and modern, of men ruined by wine, to warn himself, and called it the Classic of a Hundred Regrets. And a certain scholar Ye of Wu was by nature filial and friendly. One day after drinking he quarreled and cursed at his younger brother, and when his father came out to reason with him, he even spat out a word or two of insolence. When he woke at the fifth watch, his wife told him how he had been in his drunkenness, and his remorse and hatred were beyond bearing. He hurried to his father's room, knocked his head on the ground, wept and wailed, and knelt waiting to beg pardon, and only then did his father's anger dissolve. Ah! These two gentlemen were of mild and careful nature by habit, yet even they could not escape being perverse after drink; how much worse the case of the dissolute and depraved! Wine is well named the spring of calamity. Truly.

Wu Yu of the Song was commissioner of military affairs. At that time Chen Zhizhong was dismissed from the chancellorship and recommended Wu to take his place. At a banquet in attendance on the emperor, Wu fell asleep drunk; suddenly he stroked the couch and called for his attendants. The emperor was angry, and dismissed him to the Western Capital's retainers' office. Again Guo Zhi was assistant administrator; coming in for an audience, the smell of wine reeked over the imperial seat, and he was demoted to Nanjing.

To lose one's words after wine often brings great calamity. A certain notable of Wuxi County, young and of much talent, being drunk, exposed to a man's face the shameful secrets of his women's quarters. The man laughed easily and said: “It is only the talk of a drunkard.” He seemed not to mind in the least, and all at the table admired his forbearance. An experienced elder waited until the notable had gone, then said to those at the same table: “He who is angry is the ordinary man; he who smiles is not to be fathomed.” Half a year later the scholar was murdered by someone's plot, and all suspected that the man who held the knife was the one he had insulted before. Alas! Such are the calamities of wine. And as for falling into a river or a pit because of drink, splitting one's head or face, losing one's wealth, leaking secrets, offending the ghosts and gods — every kind of disaster and blame has wine for its cause. Why will men not give it up?

Su Yijian of the Song was a scholar of the Hanlin. Because he drank heavily he suffered a nosebleed and fell ill and died. And Wang Quan was a palace aide; from great drunkenness his navel split and he died. When the maddening drug soaks into a man, there are few who do not come down with illness; if it breaks out early the sickness is shallow, if it breaks out late the sickness is deep — but there is none it does not bring to death. Therefore, looking over all who have enjoyed a great span of years, none of them loved wine. Why will men deliver this body handed down by their forebears into a life of drunkenness and a death of dreams?

Chen Hao was fond of drink by nature and served as education commissioner of Shandong. His father sent him a letter warning him, and so he had a craftsman make a small cup and engraved words on it, saying: “By my father's command I give up wine; I shall drink only ten cups.”

The family rules of the Zheng clan of Pujiang: sons and grandsons under thirty years of age were not permitted to let wine touch their lips. Those in their prime might drink a little, but anyone who sank into drunkenness and clamor was sure to be caned. In serving guests, the only aim was sincerity and honesty; they did not force wine on them. The women of the house were not allowed to drink together; those past fifty might do as they pleased. This is fit to be a model for those who keep a household.

The ancients said: Wine means to approach. Approach what is right and one is right; approach what is wrong and one is wrong. Wine means to make. Make what is good and one is good; make what is evil and one is evil. So wine cannot of itself make a man right or wrong, good or evil; it is the man himself who makes himself right or wrong, good or evil. Can the two words “economy” and “measure” ever be dispensed with?

Zhang Gongyi of the Tang held nine generations under one roof, and it was all in a single word: forbearance. Quarreling comes of the lack of forbearance. Between flesh and blood, to insist on reason wounds the affection, and when the affection is wounded it is no longer reason. How can one quarrel rashly? Yet the source of it lies mostly in the words of women stirring up strife. For a woman's heart is not fair; she is ever nursing jealousy. And those she calls father-in-law and mother-in-law, elder and younger brothers-in-law, and sisters-in-law of her own generation, are all joined by circumstance and given their titles by force; they are not natural kindred by heaven. Therefore she makes light of cutting off affection and easily quarrels. The two sides pass each other's words back and forth until resentment piles up. Within one household discord and change spring up in clusters, and the matter has many branches that cannot be told in full. Only where the heavenly bonds are deep and true, and the man is of high and far-seeing understanding, illumining and penetrating all, will slander not be listened to; then naturally the harmonious air steams up and love and friendship are glad and full. What quarreling could there be?

Zheng Lian of Pujiang in the Ming kept a single household register for two hundred years without dividing, and men named his village the Village of Righteousness. The prefect set up a plaque over it reading: The First House Under Heaven. When Taizu came to the throne he summoned him to the capital and asked: “How many mouths does your household feed?” He answered: “A thousand and more.” The emperor said: “Truly the first house under Heaven.” At that time Empress Ma, hearing it from behind the screen, said to Taizu: “Your Majesty holds the empire, and it was one man who raised the matter. Now the Zheng family has a thousand and more in one house; would it not be easier for them to raise a matter?” The emperor was startled, and asked again: “Is there a way, sir, in your keeping the clan together?” Lian answered at once: “Nothing else — only that I do not listen to a wife's words.” The emperor could not help laughing aloud. At that time Henan presented fragrant pears, and the emperor gave him two. Lian lifted the pears in both hands above his head and hurried out. The emperor had him watched. When he reached home he called the clansmen together, faced the palace gate and knocked his head in thanks for the imperial grace, then set out two great vats of water, broke the pears into them, and gave them to all to drink. Taizu heard of it and was pleased. Later someone slandered the family for being in league with a powerful minister, and Taizu said: “The Zheng house is not like that; it is a false charge.” Later he had their sons and grandsons of thirty and above summoned to the capital and gave them all office. The clan head Ying came to the palace gate to thank him for the grace, and the emperor, at the Fengtian Gate, wrote with his own hand the three great characters “House of Filial Righteousness” and gave it to him, sealed with the imperial jade seal.

Loyalty means giving one's all to oneself; goodness is the name for uprightness. Of all things man is the most spiritual, and among men the male is held most noble. Since one has obtained this spiritual and noble body, to be treacherous and disloyal, perverse and not good, is not only to betray one's own spirit but to fail greatly toward the Creator.

Fan Zhongyan, Duke Wenzheng of the Song, lost his father at two years of age. When he was a little older he stood forth and made his own way, reciting and reading day and night, sitting still and thinking in silence, and in six years he mastered the Six Classics. At twenty he passed the imperial examination and became judge of Hezhong. His loyalty and love soaked into men's hearts. He served as vice minister and, in court and in the ordering of his household, used both kindness and authority. Loyal to his ruler and loving his country, his good deeds shine down. He taught his sons by the right way and relieved the poor and succored the suffering. His name shook his age and is revered for a hundred generations. The two words “a man” — truly he was not unworthy of them.

The Book of Rites says: The man leads, the woman follows. It says also: In youth she follows her father and elder brother; when married she follows her husband; when her husband dies she follows her son. The Family Instructions of Master Yan says: A woman's place is to preside over the kitchen and attend only to the rules of wine, food, and clothing. If she has intelligence and talent, she should only assist her husband and supply what he lacks. If she overrides her husband and meddles in affairs outside, she is the hen that crows at dawn, the owl with the long tongue, and the decline of the household begins there.

Yuan Kui of the Han married the eldest daughter of Ma Jichang, and the dowry sent with her was very rich. Kui said: “A wife's part is to hold the dustpan and broom — why need she be so overly precious and fine?” She answered: “My loving parents gave thought to it, and I did not dare defy their command. If you admire the high conduct of Bao Xuan and Liang Hong, I too will follow the righteousness of Shaojun and Meng Guang.”

Lady Hou, wife of Cheng Xiang of the Song, was modest and yielding, gentle and harmonious; even in small matters she would surely report and then act. She ordered her household by rule and did not beat the servants. If any of her sons reproved them, she would always warn him, saying: “High and low differ, but a human being is one and the same.” When Xiang was angry about something, she would always smooth it away for him. Only when her sons had faults would she not cover them, and she would often say: “A son's unworthiness comes of his mother hiding his fault, so that his father does not know of it.” Later her two sons, Yi and Hao, both became great Confucians, held high and noble office, and were offered sacrifice in the Temple of Confucius.

A certain resident of Hezhou kept more than a hundred geese. One day they ate his neighbor's rice, and the neighbor beat more than fifty of the geese to death. The man's wife saw it and was furious, but then she thought: “If I go to law with him, it will surely cost me money besides; and my husband is lying drunk, and if he learns of it and goes to beat the man, it will be even worse.” So she gathered up the dead geese and salted them. The next morning the neighbor suddenly died. When her husband learned of the day before, he was deeply moved and said: “If you had told me yesterday, I would have beaten him in my drunkenness — would that not have been a case of manslaughter?”

The Purple Mist Formula for Creating Blessing says: When a woman cultivates goodness it is no different from a man's; only, as a woman has no affairs outside the house, the three followings are her good. And if she has good deeds to do, it is best that she urge her parents and her husband to do them. Therefore, when father and mother have three good deeds, the daughter or wife takes a share of one; when the husband has two good deeds, the wife takes a share of one; and she who has thought of it beforehand shares the same merit. To urge and convert women to goodness is twice as hard and twice as meritorious as a woman doing good herself. When elder and younger sisters-in-law and sisters have good deeds, if they praise one another, their merit may be equal as well; what is precious is to rejoice with one heart and have no jealousy. If one can be filial and respectful, harmonious and yielding, assisting the husband and teaching the sons, and so fulfill one's own part, and then add to it deep faith in cause and effect, vegetarian eating, and Buddha-recitation, then in this present life body and mind will naturally be at peace and happy, sons and grandsons will flourish, and at the end of life one will surely receive the Buddha's compassionate guidance and be born in the West. One should only cultivate quietly at home and not go racing about outside: for one thing it does not waste one's time, for another it keeps one free of gossip. Again, when sons and grandsons are ill, to pray to the gods and offer sacrifice costs several pieces of silver at a stroke — how much better to do good in ordinary days and save living creatures, and so naturally obtain the gods' protection? Within the women's quarters there is a cave-heaven and a blessed land of its own. Make the effort and practice it.

When husband and wife are harmonious, the household prospers. A woman has never read books or understood principle; if she does wrong, one should clearly instruct her and make her understand. Certainly one must not let her have her own way without restraint, but neither should one at once conceive anger and loathing. Yet men of the world, meeting a fierce and violent wife, submit to her bullying; meeting a weak and simple wife, they tyrannize over her — fearing the strong and bullying the good. How can a true man do this? There are also foolish men who dote on a concubine and insult the wife, or cling to a courtesan and deceive the wife, and even beat and curse and rage at her. These above all will not come to a good end.

Yan Guangzhong said: In life let no one be born a woman's body, for every kind of sorrow and joy comes from others. She leaves her kin and parts from those she loves; in life and in death she follows another; the one she serves is her husband alone. Hungry, she does not eat alone; cold, she is not clothed alone. She gives up her own body to be mine, gives up her father and mother to be father and mother to mine. Should she light upon a merchant who travels far, or a scholar who goes abroad to study, then she keeps a lone room and sleeps alone, and on cold nights the bed is iron — is this easy to bear? And I, then, am fickle: I give my body to other houses, lodge my affection in the flowers and willows, and dote on them like a madman. Or perhaps one day I become noble and eminent, with concubines and maids before me in throngs; I give no thought to her who bound her hair with me; in fear I turn only to you, in joy I cast off the rest. Alas, why do we treat others without fellow-feeling? For the long-tongued wife who gives her will free rein and rides roughshod, and the woman of loose conduct who forgets all restraint and makes a scene, that is one thing. But when she serves her husband's parents, keeps peace with her sisters-in-law, is harmonious with her husband's aunts, and among those before and after her, wife and concubine alike, each has her own heart and all have a hand in the government of the house — her worry and vexation turning over and over, swallowing insult and choking back her voice, can scarcely be spoken of. And in a house of poverty and ruin, with no cooking-fire morning or night, she lives by her needle; there are things that cannot be told in full. How could she look to me for a lifetime, and I cast her off midway? What then of reason and feeling? This is the poem of the eastern expedition in the Juan Er — its tender feeling and gentle music, drawn out and portrayed, is the first righteousness of kingly transformation. And to delight in wife and children, to make the household peaceful, to obey father and mother — truly these are auspicious and good deeds.

Gu Kai treated his wife with propriety. Every night he entered and every morning he went out, and she seldom saw his face. When his illness grew grave, his wife came out to visit him. Kai had his attendants raise him up and put on his cap and added robes, and when he had finished expressing his care and encouragement, he at once told his wife to return. From this we see that between husband and wife, how can there be a single moment without propriety, so as to bring about the fault of excessive familiarity? Yet what else is propriety? To be harmonious and yet to have measure, to love and yet to respect each other — that is all.

Wang Balang of Luocheng was fierce by nature and loved to beat his wife. He doted on a courtesan, and the family property was all squandered. His wife being pressed by hunger and cold, he beat her the more urgently. At her wits' end, the wife asked kinsmen and neighbors to settle it between them; Balang had his wife and children live apart while he shared a room with the courtesan. Before long he fell ill and his property was exhausted, and the courtesan drifted away and left him. He went back to his wife, and his wife avoided him. He died suddenly, and his wife died too. Kinsmen and neighbors laid their two bodies in one place. In the night the sound of quarreling and cursing was suddenly heard; they opened the door and looked, and the two corpses were standing back to back.

The husband is the heaven of the wife, the one she depends on all her life. How can she not respect him? She who does not respect him is either a shrew or a loose woman; she may meet him with evil words, or curse him and work spells upon him. She does not know that to be born in a woman's body is for the most part a former condemnation; if she further wrongs her husband, she falls into the evil paths the deeper. And when the husband dies, before the flesh and bones are cold she thinks of marrying again, and looks on the sons and daughters she bore as strangers on the road. If she cannot mourn him in death, can she respect him in life?

Du Qi was a timid and weak man. His wife, Lady Zhang, always made light of him. In later years he grew sickly, and Zhang did not give him a single glance. Before long Zhang died before Qi did. After the burial the coffin burst open and she turned into a python and ran straight into the woods. Ah! The husband is the wife's heaven; to slight the husband is to slight heaven. Can heaven be slighted? Let each think on it.

In the Later Han, Liang Hong married a daughter of the Meng family named Guang. She first entered his house in finery, and for seven days Hong did not answer her. The wife then bound up her hair in a simple knot and put on plain cloth and worked as before. Hong was delighted and said: “This is truly Liang Hong's wife.” So they went together into hiding in the mountains of Baling. Later, to escape trouble, they went to Wu and lodged under the eaves of Gao Botong's house, hiring themselves out to pound grain for others. Whenever he came home, his wife would set out food for him and did not dare look up in his presence, raising the tray — that is, the bowl — level with her eyebrows. Botong said: “That hireling can make his wife respect him like this — he is no ordinary man.” So he gave them lodging in his house.

Du Gui was blind. His wife prayed day and night to the North Pole Star, and every bow was exactly seven times seven, forty-nine in number. In the end she was able to move the True Martial Lord to send down a transformation body and descend to heal him, and he could see as clearly as before.

Lady Li, wife of Yuwen Bangyan, worked hard to establish the household. She loved to read and understood the general sense of books, and with her own hand she copied and compiled passages to assist her husband; and she strictly supervised her sons in their studies. Her sons, led by Shuai, indeed passed the imperial examination and rose through the Hanlin and the Secretariat, reaching the office of Right Administration Commissioner, and their native place honored them. To this day there survives Lady Li's hand-copied collection of imperial edicts and proclamations.

Huang Guan of the Ming was a man of Anqing. In the Jianwen era he took the imperial examination as first in all three stages, and rose to be Grand Secretary. When the troops of the Jingnan campaign came, Guan died. His wife, Lady Weng, and both their daughters were taken. An order was issued that she be given to an elephant-keeper as wife. Weng made a pretext, saying that at the time of the troubles she had left a certain amount of gold in the keeping of close kin outside the city, and that if she and her children went to fetch it they would get it, but otherwise it would surely be hidden away. The elephant-keeper, greedy for the goods, went with them outside the city. The wife said: “The two girls must tie their skirts to mine for fear of losing each other in the crowd.” The slave agreed. The two girls did not understand their mother's purpose. When they came to the riverbank, she pulled the two girls and all three drowned together. To this day a temple is kept for them on the bank of the Qinhuai River.

Lady Zheng of Chongguo in the Song was the mother of Ouyang Xiu. Lord Chongguo passed the imperial examination and died while serving his second term as judge. Xiu was just four years old, and the family was poor. His mother labored with her own hands for food and clothing in order to support Xiu's study, and taught him his letters. Once on a snowy night she raked apart the cold ashes and wrote characters to teach him. In ordinary days she would weep and tell Xiu: “Your father was upright and loved to give. I did not live long enough to serve your grandparents, yet I know that your father could support his parents. I cannot know that you will succeed, yet I know that your father will have descendants. When I came to your father, it was more than a year since the mourning was ended; and at every sacrifice he would surely weep, and whenever he met with wine and meat he would surely weep, grieving that he could not support them. At first I thought it was only because he had newly put off mourning, and so for a time; but afterward it was always so, even to the end of his life, never otherwise. By this I know that your father could support his parents. Your father was an official, and once at night he was looking at the penal records and sighed again and again, saying: ‘I seek a way to let him live and cannot find it — that is what is pitiable.’ Turning his head, he saw your nurse holding you standing beside him, and he pointed at you and said: ‘My fate should be an early death; I fear I shall not live to see my son grown. You must tell him what I have said.’ In teaching his juniors he always followed this. By this I know that your father will have descendants.” Thereupon Xiu was moved to tears and strove at his studies until he passed the imperial examination and became noble and eminent, yet kept to frugality and plainness as before. Presently, for his frank remonstrance, he was demoted, and his lady said with a smile as always: “Poverty and lowliness are what we are used to. You must be at peace in it.” Xiu in the end became a worthy chancellor for his loyalty and uprightness, and his mother was many times enfeoffed as Grand Lady of Yue. Now of the ways of respecting a husband, which is greater than the two matters of fulfilling one's integrity and teaching one's sons? Therefore I place these two cases in order as the highest standard of respecting a husband. Let every wife take them to heart.

Laozi said: He who does not show himself is therefore illumined; he who does not justify himself is therefore of merit; he who does not boast of himself therefore endures. The Book of Changes says: The way of Heaven diminishes the full and benefits the modest; the way of Earth changes the full and flows toward the modest; the ghosts and gods harm the full and bless the modest. The modest is honored and shines; being lowly, it cannot be overstepped — this is the end of the gentleman. Great Yu did not boast and did not brag; foolish men and foolish women all said, “Each of us can surpass him” — yet he cut through the Dragon Gate, opened a passage at Yique, and made the earth level and Heaven complete, and his merit covered ten thousand generations. The Duke of Zhou was neither proud nor grudging; he labored in modesty and lowered himself to scholars; and in the eastern expedition he broke the ax and in the end brought peace to the house of Zhou. Therefore it is said: Truly great sages and great worthies all bring forth their work out of trembling and fear, as though standing on the brink of a deep gulf, as though treading on thin ice. Great Yu and the Duke of Zhou were sages — did they ever boast of their virtue to others? If so, then what do the men of today mean by their reckless boasting? It only shows that they do not know their own measure.

Gu Yong of the Han was enfeoffed as a marquis three days before his family knew of it. Xie An of the Jin played chess with a guest when the dispatch of victory arrived, and the guest never noticed anything. Cao Wuhui of the Song, having taken the south of the Yangtze, went in to have audience, and in the report sent up by the palace gate he wrote only that he had returned from the imperial commission to attend to public business in Jiangnan. Duke Wen Lu of the Song, in the Zhihe era, was the first to propose that Yingzong be made heir; and when Shenzong came to the throne, the duke spoke only of the merit of Han Qi, and the emperor thereby knew that he did not boast. All these gentlemen were of the very highest character and of the very greatest achievements, and still were modest and retiring and did not boast. Why do men not know to take them as their model?

He whose vessel is broad will surely have abundant blessing; he whose vessel is shallow will surely have thin blessing. Humility and fullness are the dividing line of calamity and fortune — how can one not be careful? And what is there in wealth, honor, and ability to rely upon? To be arrogant toward others with them, even apart from the calamity it brings, is first of all to lose one's heart and to know no shame.

Shi Chong of the Jin vied in wealth with Wang Kai. Kai made a purple silk screen for a march of forty li, and Chong made a brocade screen for fifty li to outdo him. Kai also once brought out a foot-long coral given him by the palace to boast before Chong, and Chong smashed it with an iron ruyi wand. Kai was furious, and Chong then brought out those he kept, all two or three feet long, and repaid him with one stalk. In other rare and precious things they contended for victory in every case. Later Chong was executed for a crime, and then he sighed, saying: “It is only that these slaves covet my wealth.” Ah! That single word of Chong's at the point of death — how clear it was! But had he known it earlier, he would surely not have boasted. Such was the cruelty of the calamity of boasting. Can the men of today be anything but careful in a single word or a single act?

Jealousy is found in both men and women. When a man sees another's rank and fame he is jealous; when he sees another's wealth and honor he is jealous; when another's position presses close to his own he resents it; when another's talent surpasses his own he resents it. All this is the working of a narrow and shallow capacity. As for women contending for favor and breeding resentment, they often bring ruin on the household and cut off its heirs, and their guilt is more than can be told. In life every man gnashes his teeth at them in hatred; in death they fall forever into hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the realm of beasts — and even so it scarcely covers their guilt. That the man should set the standard by his own person — is that not his responsibility?

Pang Juan, a general of Wei in the Zhou, was jealous of Sun Bin's talent and had his feet cut off; afterward he was killed by Bin. In the Tang, Yu Chaoen and Cheng Yuanzhen were jealous of Guo Ziyi's merit and high position and rank, and schemed and slandered to harm him again and again; in the end they all incurred guilt — Yu Chaoen was executed and Cheng was exiled. In the Song, Han Tuozhou was jealous of Zhu Wengong Xi, then a compiler of the Huanzhang Pavilion, and so he formed a faction and denounced Xi as false learning, and for a time all the gentlemen were rejected and suppressed. Later Tuozhou was executed by Shi Miyuan. Shi Mingchen of the Northern Qi all his life deeply envied anyone who came out above him; afterward in the woods he turned into a python and went off toward the valley. It is recorded that Emperor Wu of Liang obtained a formula for stopping jealousy, and his attendants offered this saying: “May Your Majesty bestow it widely upon your ministers, so that the untalented may not envy the talented, the self-seeking may not envy the self-seeking, the muddy may not envy the clear, and the greedy may not envy the honest.” This too is one branch of urging men to goodness. The emperor agreed. If so, is jealousy only a matter for women?

Nü Zong was the wife of Su Bao of the Song in the Zhou. She served her mother-in-law with great filial piety. Su took office in Wei and after three years married a wife abroad. Her husband's elder brother's wife told her of it, and Nü Zong said: “A woman takes single-mindedness as her chastity and good compliance as her obedience. How could taking sole possession of her husband's love be her goodness? By the rites, a great officer may have three, and a knight two. My husband is a knight; that he has two, is it not fitting? Moreover, a wife may be put away for seven causes, and jealousy is the first of them. You do not tell me the rules of the household, but instead would have me commit an act that gets me cast off?” When the Duke of Song heard of it, he had her gate honored with a plaque and named her Nü Zong.

Lu Bian's uncle was magistrate of Hucheng, and Bian went to visit him. In a dream he came to a place where there were ten great millstones, and around the millstones were countless women. The millstones turned by themselves, and the ox-headed guards scooped up the women with great winnowing baskets and cast them into the hole of the mill, and they came out with the grinding, their bones and flesh crushed to powder, and the sound of their pain was hard to hear. Among the crowd Bian saw his uncle's wife, the wife of the magistrate of Hucheng. They met with grief and joy, and Bian asked for what cause these suffered such punishment. She said: “For jealousy.” Ah! So does hell requite jealousy. Dreadful, dreadful.

Liang Renyu favored a servant girl. His wife, Lady Li, was jealous and cruel: she bound the girl and beat her on the head. The girl cried out: “I am a servant of low birth, with no control over myself. Why must you lock my neck in irons and torment me so cruelly?” More than a month after the servant girl died, Lady Li fell ill, and the girl tormented her constantly. Four sores broke out on her head, and she wailed and screamed, and her skull rotted away and she died.

Guo, the wife of Jia Chong of the Jin, was jealous by nature. She once bore a son, and the wet nurse held him, and Chong went to him and stroked him. Guo had the wet nurse whipped to death. The child missed his nurse and wept himself to death. In the end Chong had no heir. Jia Chong was a great villain who ruined the state, and so a jealous wife cut off his line — this is the way of Heaven. Yet in the world those whose lines are cut off through jealousy are indeed not few. Let such a jealous wife give no thought to the depth of her sin and the greatness of her evil, and to the retribution of hell she cannot escape; but does she never think of the desolate grave of her line cut off before her eyes, the bones scattered, wind and rain grieving over the soul in the dark terrace, cattle and sheep trampling the pasture, and at the Cold Food Festival and Qingming, who will pour out a cup of water? Wild mist and rank grass, and ghosts weeping in the chill — for what cause is this? How sad! When my words come to this, I cannot but grieve and ache on behalf of such people, and cry aloud and sigh long. Let every wife think of it while there is yet time. Yet let me look again at the case of Jia Chong: that his line was cut off was the way of Heaven; and that a jealous wife came forth from his house was also a cunning turn of evil retribution. How can the husband then fail to think of piling up virtue to turn back Heaven, and instead only blame the jealousy of the woman?

In the Later Wei, the wife of Du Chang was Lady Liu. She was exceedingly jealous. There was a servant girl named Jinjing; when Chang bathed, he had her comb his hair, and Liu cut off both her fingers. Before long Liu was stung by a fox's spine, and both her fingers fell off. There was another servant girl named Yulian who could sing, and Chang loved her, and Liu cut out her tongue. Later Liu's own tongue rotted with sores, and when the matter became urgent she went to Chan Master Chou to repent. The master said: “You, madam, cut off a servant girl's fingers, and your own fingers have fallen; you cut out a servant girl's tongue, and your own tongue is severed. If you repent with a sincere heart, then you may escape.” Lady Liu bowed in worship and begged for mercy. After seven days the Chan master had her open her mouth wide and recited a spell over her. Two snakes came out of her mouth, more than a foot long; he recited the spell urgently, and they fell to the ground, and her tongue was restored. And from then on she was no longer jealous. Now when a man repents and mends his evil, gods and men alike are glad. However boundless the karma of sin you have made, only repent from now on and do not repeat it, and the former guilt melts like ice in a moment. This case is clear proof. To take warning from it and repent is truly a great blessing.

Alas! The resentful wife has no good end, for a woman's feelings are easily knotted. Therefore cruel, venomous, and treacherous deeds she does in her own person without hesitation. It rests with the parents and brothers of the woman's own house: if she is not yet married, to guide her beforehand; if she is married, to restrain her with tact and not to feed her flame. Then perhaps the heart of jealousy may be somewhat stilled. And to mediate and transform her from within is the husband's part. As for him who pursues women and gives rein to lust, so that the lion of the eastern river roars, the gentleman will hold that the guilt of the lewd husband is by far the lighter.

Treat a wife with harmony and respect; treat a son with strictness and uprightness. To treat a wife without propriety is to lose the meaning of husband and wife as one answering the other; to teach a son without the Way is to wound the grace of engendering and rearing him. To be unrighteous and unkind is altogether to be without conduct. Those who treat their wives today: if not harsh and stingy with affection, then overfamiliar without measure. Those who treat their sons: if not too indulgent, then certainly too severe. When one has no conduct oneself, how can one reprove wife and son?

Zhang Zhan of the Later Han was grave and strict and loved propriety; in his daily conduct he was always respectful. Whenever he met with his wife and sons he would set forth the instructions of propriety and good words and excellent deeds to teach them, like a stern lord governing his ministers. Therefore his wife also admonished him and improved herself in turn, and their good name was heard in the district. This case may serve well as a model for teaching wife and sons.

Shi Tang married while still of low estate. When he passed the imperial examination, he resented that he had not got a daughter of a rich house for a wife, and repented of it. So day by day he kept apart from her and no longer slept in the same bed. His wife's heart grew heavy and she fell ill. For several years Tang did not give her a single glance, and his wife too swallowed her resentment. As she was dying she called to Tang through the wall, saying: “I am dying now. Can you bear not to look at me once?” Tang never turned to look. A year after his wife's death, the courts of the underworld condemned him for his wicked and heartless conduct and cut away his years and emoluments, and he died of a sudden illness.

Wang Yao of Zhuozhou doted on his two sons and fostered vicious natures in them; unable to control them, he reported them to the officials. Both sons died, and his line was cut off. When Yao died, on the night of the fifteenth day of the second month of the following year, Liu Jin, a temple attendant at the local City God's temple, saw a man holding a petition and begging for offerings at Qingming. The City God said angrily: “You had sons and could not teach them, and you cut off your own line yourself. Who can make offerings to you?” He ordered the ghost guards to drive him out. The man went off weeping aloud. The temple keeper inquired after him the next day, and learned that Yao had been dead more than a year. The old saying goes: The sons of Confucius' house did not know how to curse; the sons of Zengzi's house did not know how to quarrel — habit had made their nature. It says also: Raise sons and younger brothers as you raise the orchid and the angelica: you pile up learning to cultivate them and pile up goodness to moisten them. Between father and son one must not dote with a small tenderness; from youth restrain them with strictness and bind them with law, and then when grown they will not bring the regret of unworthiness. It says also: When a man has several sons, the love shown in food and clothing must not be unequal; the distinction of elder and younger, honored and humble, must not be slack; the difference between worthy and unworthy, right and wrong, must not be undiscerned. Show them equality when young, and when grown they will have no trouble of contending over wealth; reprove them with strictness when young, and when grown they will have no trouble of insolence and contempt; teach them to distinguish when young, and when grown they will have no trouble of joining evil company. Looking over all these sayings together, a man may know what to take as his model.

A wife should serve her husband's father and mother exactly as a son serves his own father and mother: with a lowly spirit and a cheerful countenance and a soft voice, sharing their warmth and cold in her own body, feeling their sickness and pain and itch and ache as her own concern, supporting them in going out and coming in. If she fails in propriety even a little, that is unfilial, and the guilt of it reaches to Heaven, and thunder and fire will strike at once. Ah! But I have something further to say. A wife is joined to her husband's parents by man; a son is joined to his parents by Heaven. From ancient times, a son who is unfilial to his parents while the wife alone is filial to her husband's parents — I fear there is no such principle. Therefore every failure of propriety in a wife is brought about by her husband. Would the gods' punishment and the ghosts' censure fall upon the woman alone? Let every son take this to heart.

On the twenty-second day of the third month of the fifth year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming, in Shanyang County of Huai'an, Feng, the wife of Mao Jizong, was filial by nature to the utmost. Her mother-in-law was old and gravely ill, and Mao was away transporting grain to the capital. The wife bathed and changed her clothes, and at night cried out to Heaven to die in her mother-in-law's place. She took a knife and cut into her own side, and the tip of her liver sprang out. Suddenly she heard her child cry; fearing it would wake her mother-in-law, she covered the wound with a kerchief and went in to soothe the child. Then, thinking that so small a piece of liver would not be enough to heal her, she prayed devoutly and cut again. The moon had not yet risen, when the sky suddenly became bright and clear and the stars all shone, lighting the wife's body as bright as day. She cut a leaf of liver from her belly and at once made it into broth and brought it to her mother-in-law. As soon as the old woman tasted it she felt it wondrously sweet, and asked what it was. The wife made the excuse that a neighbor had got a deer: it was deer's liver. The old woman ate it all, and her illness healed at once. So it was that her utmost sincerity moved Heaven, and the wound did not pain her; but the traces of blood could not be hidden. Her husband's younger sister noticed it, and the whole household was astonished and told of it. Only then did her mother-in-law know that she had saved her. She wept bitterly and was moved and pitied her. For a time the scholars and gentlemen of the district joined in a petition to the throne, but through the exactions of the petty clerks it could not reach the emperor. Happily there was Jiang Tianyi, a licentiate of Huizhou, who wrote A Collection of Wondrous Filial Piety Shaking Heaven to make the matter known.

Jia Dan of the Song was military commissioner of Huazhou. At that time there was a woman of the people who served her mother-in-law unfilial. The mother-in-law was old and blind, and the woman served her foul food. The old woman wondered at its taste, and when her son came home from outside he took it and questioned his wife. When the son saw it he wept aloud toward Heaven, and suddenly thunder crashed and a swift stroke cut off the woman's head and joined a dog's head to her body. Dan learned of it and had her led about within the borders of the province as a warning to the unfilial. Alas, alas! Men today are quick to say that a woman is of watery nature and cannot be established in teaching. How far this saying is from reason! Nowadays, in the days when she is a girl, her parents have already failed in the method of teaching and rearing; and when she is a wife, her foolish husband lacks the benefit of a model to observe. Thus the evils of disobedience, lewdness, and jealousy come to seem impossible to restrain. But if those who are her parents, from childhood to the binding of her hair, would open her heart with filial piety, respect, gentleness, and compliance, then even though she marry a man without talent, she could still know how to establish herself; how much more when the one who sets her the pattern is a filial, brotherly, good, and kind gentleman! The teaching of daughters and the teaching of sons are of equal weight — this saying should truly be made known to all the world.

The ancestral spirits are the spirits of one's forebears. Whenever the dressing of the dead and the encoffining are without propriety, the mourning without rule, the burial not made in due time, the fasting and sacrifice not sincere, the sweeping of the graves not diligent, the ancestral hall not kept in order, and the incense and lamp broken and intermittent — all these are slights. Now the water has its source and the tree its root: how dare one forget them even for a moment? If one fails in this, I do not know what can be said for him.

Crown Prince Zhaoming of Liang was of the utmost goodness and filial piety. When Lady Ding the Consort, who bore him, died, he would not let water or gruel pass his lips, and at every bout of weeping he fainted away. Emperor Wu instructed him, saying: “Grief must not destroy the nature. I am here — how can you carry on so?” Only then did the crown prince force himself to take a few mouthfuls; and from that time to the burial he took a pint of wheat gruel a day. The crown prince's body had always been stout, and his belt measured ten spans; by this time he had wasted away by more than half. Whenever he went in to court, officials and common folk who saw him could not but weep.

Chen Gao came to the capital as a tribute student and prayed for a dream at a temple of the gods. In the dream a god said to him: “Your father's coffin is not yet buried. Rank and fame are not to be asked about yet.” Chen did not believe it. The next year he was failed at the examination hall, and so he went home and hurried to complete the burial. When he took the examination again, he passed at last. The Ledger of Merits and Demerits says: He who does not bury his parents within three years of their death, for each month of delay incurs ten demerits. He who buries them without doing his utmost, or lets the grave be damaged, incurs a hundred demerits. He who does not mend it at once after becoming aware, for each day of delay incurs ten demerits. It says also: To sacrifice to one's forebears at the wrong season and without reverence incurs one demerit; and if it is because of pleasure-seeking that the season is missed, that is five times more.

Whenever Deng Zuoming swept the graves, he would linger in the graveyard and return only after a whole day, saying: “In the space of a year, how many days do I come here? I cannot bear to go away as if it did not matter.” Words of the utmost goodness! Nowadays, by the custom of the world, once at the year's festivals and at Qingming one visits the graves, and the rest of the time one leaves one's parents in the wild waste and gives them no thought. At the sacrifice one mostly joins with brothers, kinsmen, and friends in giving free rein to pleasure and roaming, and returns having enjoyed it to the full. The year's festival is no sweeping of the pines; it is only admiring the plum blossom. Qingming is no visiting of the graves; it is only treading the green. Alas! If emolument does not reach one's parents, what good is it to fill wife and children? If in life one stinted them of coarse food and water, what use is it to set out the full array of tripods after death?

A minister receives his charge from his lord; a son from his parent; a disciple from his teacher. All who stand below and receive their charge from those above — it is the charge of a superior. If what is commanded cannot rightly be done, one should still bend every effort to move him and remonstrate beforehand; then one has not dared to accept the charge. If what is commanded may rightly be done, then to carry it out without effort is still a fault — how much more to defy it? Defiance is where rebellious ministers and traitorous sons come from.

Tao An of the Ming was a man of Dangtu. Taizu appointed An magistrate of Huangzhou, instructing him: “Cherish well the common folk.” An reverenced the imperial charge. When he came to the prefecture he remitted taxes and corvée, lightened heavy labor, diligently instructed the scholars, and reduced punishments and penalties, and the people all rejoiced and submitted. He was recalled to be a Hanlin scholar and promoted to the Jiangxi provincial administration as assistant administrator. In whatever had no cause for evasion he gave his whole heart and strength to match the imperial charge. When An died, the emperor himself composed a text to sacrifice to him, granted him a posthumous title, and extended the privilege to his sons; his sons and grandsons all passed the imperial examination and rose to the offices of ministers and assistants. Now those today who are to cherish and govern the black-haired people all look up to and receive the charge of their ruler. Yet they are cruel and tyrannical toward living beings and do injury to the common folk, giving not the least thought to our ruler's heart of teaching and rearing — what guilt of defiance could exceed this? The common folk can indeed do nothing about it. But do they know that Heaven's mirror is not far, that the people may not be tyrannized over, and Heaven may not be cheated?

All things in the world turn to emptiness in a moment. Only the piling up of virtue and the doing of good, the promoting of benefit and the removing of harm, and matters of that kind — world after world and life after life — go with one and are enjoyed, without end. Other things, such as mansions and terraces and ponds, clothes and food and carriages and horses, and all the affairs of poetry, painting, and rare curiosities, are all enough to lose one's purpose and burden the body. What good are they? As for hanging lanterns and putting on plays, singing songs and drinking wine, and games of chance and chess and the like, not only are they of no benefit — they are among the greatest harms. Shun them, shun them.

Zhang Yong of the Song, when he governed Chengdu, feared that the people would find food hard to come by and turn to banditry. He had the land tax of the various districts commuted to six hundred thousand hu of rice each year; and when spring came he would register the common folk, allotting each by the number of mouths a certificate to buy rice at the original price. By this means, even in years of famine and poor harvest, there was no great hunger. Chen Yaozuo was grain transport commissioner of Guangnan. It was the custom there not to take medicine: when ill, the people prayed to ghosts, and many died. The commissioner gathered tested prescriptions from his own household and had them carved in stone at the post stations, and the local people relied on them. Wang Di was magistrate of Chengdu. Many of the people practiced cremation, and the commissioner strictly forbade it, setting aside official land for public graveyards to bury the unburied, and from that the region had no more cremation. Su Shi was magistrate of Hangzhou. He dredged the two rivers, repaired the six wells, and built a long embankment planted with willows to secure the embankment's benefit, and the people named it the Su Embankment. Yu Zhongkuan was magistrate of Shunchang. The custom there was much drowning of infant girls. The commissioner wrote an exhortation and warning, summoned the elders to the veranda, earnestly comforted and encouraged them, and brought out the text to urge them, and the custom was wholly changed. All those above did what was beneficial. From this we know that a gentleman in the world values what benefits men and things; how could he merely talk grandly and argue broadly without practical result? As for us in cultivating our persons and rectifying ourselves and examining our past faults, there is truly more work than the days can hold; yet men recklessly undertake all kinds of useless doings, not knowing that this phantom body and phantom world in a flash return to extinction, and that only the one perfectly bright nature endures through ten thousand kalpas, never born and never dying. Why do men today, rather than idly whiling away the hours, dragging through water and mud, not do a little work within this?

A minister who cheats his lord, a son who defies his parent, a wife who turns her back on her husband, brothers who plunder each other, friends who undermine each other — all are the working of an outer heart. And it need not take shape in deed: as soon as a subtle stirring arises, men may not know it, but the ghosts and gods have already condemned the heart.

Qin Hui of the Song schemed in secret with the men of Jin and strove to uphold a peace settlement. Whenever our generals won a slight victory, he at once pressed them to withdraw their armies, and the cities and towns we gained were lost again immediately. He also had Yue Fei killed in prison. Later there was one who went to the underworld and saw Hui in the uninterrupted hell. Today, before the tomb of the Prince of Yue in Hangzhou, iron statues of Hui and his wife kneel; visitors beat them and urine on them to vent their hatred.

A certain man of Yuezhong in the Ming treated his wife with deep affection. But the wife came to long for a youth of the neighborhood, and the two would look at each other from time to time. Though she dwelt in the same room with her husband, her heart thought only of the youth. Later her husband fell ill and died, and before the mourning was ended she married the youth. That night she dreamed that her former husband came and said: “That you married after my death I do not reproach. But that while I lived you cherished an outer heart — that is truly hateful.” Thereupon he took an iron mallet and struck her on the back, and soon after she vomited blood and died.

This sentence speaks of cursing when there is no right to seek vindication: whenever in anger a man curses himself and also curses others. This is the first omen of disaster called down by the petty man and the woman, and often before death comes, what they have cursed comes to pass at once. How can one not take warning?

The wife of Yan Dian had once been intimate with another man and had also stolen a handkerchief from a neighbor's house. The neighbor cursed and reviled her, and Dian then cursed himself and cursed the other, saying: “If my wife has indeed been intimate with a man and stolen your handkerchief, may I be struck by lightning; and if not, then you must take it.” Before long Dian was struck dead by the thunderbolt's axe, and beneath his ribs were written the words: “The fool protects his wife.” His wife too was struck dead, and beneath her ribs were written the words: “She practiced lewdness and stole.”

Zihan of the state of Zheng in the Zhou said: To have oaths and curses is the root of disorder. Now life and death have their fixed decree: it is not what one loves that can give life, nor what one hates that can kill. Yet men today curse themselves and curse others — how deluded, how foolish!

Partial hatred and partial love have a very wide reach. In every case — the lord toward his minister, the father toward his son, the husband toward wife and concubine, the master toward his servants — it is found. But among women it is worst between those before and after her and between wife and concubine. Therefore Zengzi, when his wife died, did not marry again for the rest of his life, saying: “Emperor Gaozong, because of a second wife, brought about the death of Xiaoji; Yin Jifu, because of a second wife, brought about the death of Boqi. I am not the equal of Gaozong above, nor the match of Jifu in the middle; how could I be free of the same fault?” Excellent! This is one who feared to have partial hatred and partial love, and so preserved a father's grace whole. Yet not to marry again after a wife's death is what human feeling finds hard. Let one only seek, after marrying again, always to realize Zengzi's words; then perhaps one will not go greatly astray.

Xu Jia of the Eastern Sea had by his former wife, Lady Xu, a son named Tiejie. When Xu died, he married again, a Lady Chen, who was fierce and jealous and wished to kill the son of the former wife. Chen bore a son, and named him Tiechu — the iron pestle — meaning to pound the mortar, Tiejie. Tiejie was given over to every kind of beating, and died of cold and hunger at the age of sixteen. More than ten days after his death, his ghost suddenly came home and said: “I am Tiejie. My mother has appealed her grievance to Heaven and obtained a warrant from the celestial court to come and wipe out the wrong. Let Tiechu die of sickness, and let him suffer as I suffered.” Chen tried a hundred schemes to avert it, and could not. At that time Tiechu was six years old. Suddenly his belly swelled and his body ached, and his whole body turned black and purple, and he died.

In the Zhou of the Northern Wei there was a compassionate mother, a daughter of the Mengyang family, who was the second wife of Mang Mao. She bore three sons, and her husband's former wife had left five sons, none of whom loved the mother; yet the mother treated them most generously, and still the five sons did not love her. The compassionate mother then had it that her own three sons should not be ranked with the former wife's sons: in clothing and food, in rising and resting, in advancing and withdrawing, they were kept far apart. Still the five sons of the former wife did not love her. Before long the middle son of the former wife broke the command of the King of Wei and was condemned to death. The compassionate mother grieved and lamented, and toiled morning and evening to save him. Someone said: “The son does not love the mother, and that to the utmost. Why do you labor and fear for him like this?” The compassionate mother said: “My own sons, even if they do not love me, I must still save them from calamity and rid them of guilt. Now toward the former wife's son it is otherwise: how would that differ from having no mother at all? His father, because the boy was orphaned, made me his stepmother. A stepmother is a mother to him; if she does not love her son, can she be called compassionate? To be fond of one's own and neglect those who came before — can that be called righteous? Uncompassionate and unrighteous, how could I stand in the world? Though he does not love me, can I recklessly forsake righteousness?” So she persuaded the King of Wei, who admired her righteousness and pardoned the son and restored his household. From that time the five sons drew close to the compassionate mother in affection, harmonious as though of one mother. And she trained and guided the eight sons by propriety and righteousness, and all of them became great officers and ministers of Wei.

To overstep is to stride across. A well benefits and succors very widely; it has a spring god presiding over it, named Guan, whose form is like a beautiful woman. And the water in a well both profits the multitude of living beings and is used besides to sacrifice to the gods and make offerings to the Buddhas — how can it be profaned? The stove is one of the five sacrifices; it is the Great One, the Fire God, surnamed Zhang, named Zhuo, styled Ziguo. He governs the lives of high and low in a single household; he specially observes the length and shortness of good and evil, and foreknows good and ill fortune. To overstep it is to profane and insult the divine spirits, and the guilt of it is very great. And this is not only striding over it: to sit on the well-curb, to tread on the stove door, to dry foul things over it, and the like, are all defilements and profanations.

Zhang Xiaoxian, when drunk with wine, loved to jump into wells for sport. One day a golden-armored god in the well thrust at him with a spear, and Xiaoxian's belly pained him greatly, constantly as though pierced by a lance. Only after devout prayer did he heal.

Wu Zhan of the Qing dynasty was a county clerk. His dwelling stood beside the Jing Stream. The stream had a spring, exceedingly clear, and all the clerks relied upon it. Wu Zhan built a fence to shield and protect it, so that no filth might enter. One day, beside the spring, he found a white snail and put it in a jar. Each time he came home from outside, food and drink in the kitchen were already prepared. His heart was greatly astonished. One day he secretly peeped in: it was a woman, who came forth from the snail and worked with her own hands. Wu Zhan hurried toward her; the woman, greatly flustered, had no time to return into the shell, and told him the truth, saying: I am the spirit of the spring. The Most High, because you reverently protected the source of the spring, and knowing that you dwelt as a widower, commanded me to prepare your meals. If you eat my meals, you shall attain the Way. With these words she vanished.

Han Yin Zifang was a man of the utmost filial piety, and had a benevolent and kindly heart as well. It happened that on the winter sacrifice day, while the morning meal was being cooked, the Kitchen God suddenly appeared before him. Zifang bowed twice, and thereafter, whenever the winter sacrifice day came round, he offered sacrifice to him. From this he grew very rich, equal to a lord of the land. In time his grandson Yin Shi had a daughter who became empress, and the family obtained a fief as marquises. For this reason the descendants of the Yin clan sacrificed to the hearth god generation after generation.
Xiang Lin was by nature half mad. One day, sitting on the plank roof north of the hearth, he dreamed that the Lord of the Hearth rebuked him, and his family was ruined and scattered at once.
Food is the resource by which life is nourished. Man is one of the Three Powers; how can he make light of it? If one leaps over it, it is in every case a sin. How can one fail to take warning?

In the Tang dynasty an official went into the mountains until he reached a lonely, inaccessible place, where he saw a wineshop. He bought wine and drank it. A woman first took his money and went inside; after a long while she came out carrying wine, whose color was like blood, and which tasted very sweet. He wished to drink again, and the woman, weeping, told him: I am no living person. Because in my life I was extravagant without measure, drinking wine without restraint, and would often tread underfoot leftover soup and scraps of meat and then give them to others to eat, I have received this retribution. Whenever someone buys wine, I must draw out the blood of my own body to supply it. The official, greatly frightened, turned back. How could there be a wineshop on a high mountain? One may suppose that this official had always been careless about food and drink, and that the underworld borrowed this to warn and reform him.

Zhai Lin of the Song dynasty once escorted Master Zhengshu on his westward journey. On the road they lodged at a monastery. The place where he sat happened to have its back to a holy image. The master said: Turn your chair; do not sit with your back to it. Lin said: Is it not that we should reverence it because his disciples revere him? The master said: Whenever a thing bears human form and countenance, one should not treat it with disrespect. Guishan heard of this and greatly admired his words, saying with delight: If one does not presume to slight even that which resembles a man, then how much more toward a man himself! This shows it plainly. If to turn one's back is already not permitted, how much less to leap over it?

The human body is supremely precious, and to obtain a human body is supremely difficult. The Buddha said that when a person is about to be born, the Minister of the Nine Heavens is in the court, the Nine Heavens offer congratulations, Taiyi holds the tally, the Lord Emperor ranks the destiny, the Master of Registers inscribes the record, the Master of Destinies fixes the reckoning, the Five Emperors oversee the birth, the Holy Mother guards the chamber, and the gods of heaven and the spirits of earth of the three realms all stand watch. To be restored to the human path, to be lifted into the form of the Great Yang — it alarms heaven and startles earth; its preciousness cannot be spoken of. What fault had you to repay, that you dared kill it? A woman who runs off in lust, conceives, and then procures abortion is worse than a beast; there is no reasoning with her. There are even those who, being poor, grow weary of many children; or who destroy the child once it is born; or who procure abortion before it is born. The karma of killing man cannot be repented or redeemed. The lives of creatures are most minute, and yet men still wish to set them free and keep the precept against killing — how much more for sons and daughters? That men in this one life have no son, or bear a child that does not live, or in old age see their sons die before them — all this is the retribution drawn down by having made such evil karma in former lives.

Qian Bangwei, magistrate of Guixi, found that by the custom of the place, when a daughter was born she was very often not raised. He therefore set forth for the people the right rule of conduct, and strictly enforced reward and punishment: whoever killed a daughter, five households should be punished together for it. By this means those who were kept alive could not be numbered. Bangwei afterward became prefect of Tingzhou, enjoyed a great age, and his sons and grandsons all flourished. Now for forbidding the destroying of the unborn and the casting away of the born, he obtained such a recompense as this. Men of today ought at every turn to exhort and instruct the people: the merit of it is no small thing.

Guo Yin had a daughter named Yinfeng. She was seized and dragged away by two ghosts, and made to pass through all eighteen hells. In the last hell, a king sat upon the throne in the hall, and below him were ranged several hundred women, each with a small child that clung to her legs, wailing and demanding its life. Some had drowned their daughters because they had borne too many; some, being poor, had not raised the child once it was born; some, when a wife grew jealous that a concubine had borne a son, had beaten the child to death in the womb; some had poisoned a child conceived in secret; some had injured it in a quarrel; some had beaten and flung it until it died because they were angered by its crying; some, through careless watching, had let the child die before its time. The king questioned them one by one, and not one of them was without shackles on her body; they were withered and thin, and piteous to see. When Yinfeng had returned, she told her father all of it, and he therefore wrote a great inscription on the wall of Tianning Monastery as a warning.

The woman Yang Asheng had been poor and sickly from childhood, and in her later years was in still worse straits. As she was dying she spoke to herself, saying: In a former life I was a physician. I failed in careful examination. A woman said she was ill with a worm in her belly, and I could not distinguish that she was with child. I hastily gave her yuanhua wine to bring it away, and the woman died together with the two children in her womb. Thus by one act I killed three people. The officers of the underworld held me guilty, and when my suffering was complete, I was punished with the body of a woman. Now it is already the third time, and life after life I am forever a base slave, long bound in hunger and thirst, often sick and seldom at ease. You may tell the physicians of the world to take me for a warning. With these words she died.

Emperor Wen said: When a man's son is unfilial, there are in truth the statutes of Heaven by which he is put to death. But to kill a child that has done no wrong is to kill the people of the whole world. And if a man wishes to kill a child, why does he not restrain his desire? Yet he dares to kill a man and give it no thought. In this present age, how can one be sure that such people do not exist? I have seen those who suffer punishment in Fengdu, and very many of them have committed this offense. Let all men quickly awake and repent; do not hasten the chastisement of Heaven.
He Longtu's Song of Warning Against Drowning Daughters says:
The tiger and the wolf are fiercest in nature, yet still they know that there are father and son.
Man is the soul of all the myriad things; how is he then less than these?
Whether a son is born or a daughter, held at the breast they are but one and the same.
I hear that when a daughter is killed, the pain of it is past compare.
The afterbirth blood is still running down; her mouth has no words to speak.
She wails in the water of the basin, and only after a long while comes to die.
Alas, how can a parent's heart be cruel to such a degree?
Therefore I exhort our people: never kill your daughters.
A thornwood pin and a hempen skirt will hardly make you poor.
A woman's nature is softest and most kind; she loves her kin more than her sons.
A son is often away from home; a daughter stays beside her parents.
A son is often stubborn and cross; a daughter is ever obedient to her parents.
A son is often far abroad; a daughter stays near her parents.
A son has little grief; a daughter weeps for her parents.
A daughter has a heart of filial love, and again and again she saves her parents.
When a daughter finds a worthy husband, again and again she brings her parents honor.
Do you not see Tiying, that girl, who freed her father from the pain of mutilation?
Do you not see Tang Xiang, that girl, who saved her father by seizing the tiger?
Qin, at the age of eighteen, brought her father's body home for burial.
Cao E, at the age of fourteen, dived into the river to find her father's corpse.
Shuxian grieved that her father drowned, and clasped the corpse and floated on the water.
Yuan's daughter, whose mother was palsied, when the fire came could not rise.
The girl wept and could not bear to flee; she chose to burn to death with her mother.
A Song girl was known as Chen San; her parents were poor as washed-out rags.
The three sisters shared their gruel, living wholly on water chestnut gleanings.
When her parents died she would not marry, but kept their grave until her teeth fell out.
A Tang girl, Yu Hezi, whose father and brother both fell in war.
Hezi was just seventeen; barefoot she walked to the far frontier.
A beggar, she carried the bones home, and paid for the burial by her weaving.
She cut her hair and marred her face, and then kept watch at the grave.
Her great fidelity reached the emperor's ear; a decree proclaimed her gate.
Filial indeed was the lady of the Xiao house; her parents died in a foreign land.
The lady was but sixteen years old, and she bore the coffin home to her village.
The boatman cheated her in her loneliness, and abandoned the coffin on the way.
She gathered earth with her hands and heaped a tomb, the lady with only one maid beside her.
She marred her face and mourned day and night, and built her hut by the waterside.
When the mourning was full she would not put it off; when suitors came she would not wed.
Whoever could bring back the coffin, to him alone she would give herself.
And indeed she married the man who brought the coffin back, an old lieutenant of Yangshe.
The daughter of the Tu family of Dongwu; her father was blind and crippled with palsy.
The house had no grain for the next night's meal; kin and neighbors all cast them off.
The girl then moved her two parents far away to a hempen hut.
By day she gathered wood and traded for grain; by night she spun hemp and traded for wadding.
Her two parents at last fulfilled their years; she carried earth and made their grave.
She kept the grave and never married, only because she had no brother.
Of the wise and filial women of old, how many there are, past all recording.
Some were given gold by the officers; some were honored with imperial gifts.
Some became consorts of princes; some became the wives of lords.
If a man can keep another's life alive, the recompense should not go astray.
I exhort the people of the world: better return to the Way of Heaven.
Do not say an infant girl is foolish, and does not know to resent and repay.
If a daughter's life her own kin will not pity, how can they be sure to pity their own lives?
No heir, and years cut short: fearful is the law of the underworld.
And when the day comes to demand a life, it is too late to gnaw one's navel in regret.
Why not keep her whole and living, so that both bone and flesh win blessing?

Hidden and secret — this is not one thing only. Such matters as lewdness, theft, and licentiousness, and all that cannot be known by Heaven or spoken before men, are of this kind. But the greatest of them must belong to the deeds of lust. This is why the Most High wrote this passage after the injuring of children and the procuring of abortion. Surely there is a reason for it.

Mao Qizong said: North of the town of Fuliang there lived Zhang Mingsan, who followed his father to official post in Qiongya. The government quarters adjoined the residence of Commander Li. Li had two daughters, both beautiful, and Mingsan carried on illicit relations with them. When he returned home he secretly took the two girls along in his boat, intending to cross the sea. Li pursued him in hot haste; at his wits' end, Mingsan shoved both girls into the water. Ten years later Mingsan fell ill with lumbago and engaged a physician named Sun to treat him. The medicine brought slight relief, but that night Sun dreamed he was fishing at the Mei in his village, and in the seawater stood two women, naked, who seized his robe and said: "We are from Qiong. We came to cure Zhang of his sickness. Will you really rob us of our merit?" With that they dragged Sun into the water. He woke in a cold sweat that soaked his back. At dawn he told what he had seen, and Mingsan, beating his breast, sighed: "My karma has caught up with me. I am as good as dead." Indeed he died within the month. Here is a case of a man and women whose deeds were deeply hidden, and who each in turn received their retribution. Mingsan and the two girls first met in secret and then fled in secret; the girls in the end died by Mingsan's hand, and Mingsan in the end died by the spirits of the two girls. One may call this retribution most cunning and yet never leaking. On the whole, to violate another man's wife or daughter and to wreck another man's official career are the two things most often done in hiding and most destructive of the human heart and of Heaven's principle. Therefore he who violates the wives and daughters of others will have his own wife and daughter violated, and he who wrecks the career of others will have his own career wrecked. As the saying goes: In a dark room the heart may fail, but the divine eye is as lightning. How can one not take heed?

Hui means the last day of the month, when the Director of Fate and the Kitchen God memorialize the merits and faults of the world's people. La means the five la days, when the Heavenly Lords of the five qi assemble to reckon the good and evil of the living. On those days the Heavenly Lords hold audience at the Mystic Capital and govern the human world, the underworld, the Five Peaks, and the thirty-six thousand spirits of yin and yang; they determine each person's good and evil, guilt and blessing, honor, emolument, and allotted years, and all matters of fortune and misfortune, life and death, entering each one in the registers. The first day of the first month is called the Heaven La; the fifth day of the fifth month, the Earth La; the seventh day of the seventh month, the La of the Way and Its Virtue; the first day of the tenth month, the Year La; the eighth day of the twelfth month, the Prince La. Whoever meets such a day and has committed even one fault has it written in the black register — can he atone for his guilt? Moreover, on these days the Northern Emperor of Fengdu and the Heavenly Lord of the Great Yin bring forth the long-departed ancestors, parents, and kin of the living, and even the ghost souls in the dark prisons, and question them: how many years have they dwelt in the realm of darkness, what piled-up crimes and tangled feuds brought them to this pass, where now stand their graves, and who are their descendants by name? Once the names of descendants, brothers, kin, and the nine clans are obtained, they are gathered and assessed, and these become the record of the living person's guilt. If through piled-up kalpas no one has offered deliverance, the burden is surely extended to the living. Moreover on these days the spirits of the departed kin are all released and each returns to the family home to receive offerings. As descendants, one ought to rely on the methods of the Way to sacrifice and to ransom them. To give oneself over to singing and dancing is to offend Heaven, Earth, and the ancestors. On the hui and la days, then, should one offer deliverance, or should one sing and dance?

Huaiyin's Qiang Fu was careful in conduct all his life and modest and gentle in his dealings. On the first and fifteenth of each month and on the la days he read and recited the Sanskrit scriptures and bowed in worship to the spirits, never slackening from first to last. It happened that on the New Year's Day, the Heaven La, a petty fellow got drunk and reviled him. Fu shut his door and paid no heed.
